laws.title: Pico y Placa — Driving Restrictions by Plate Number
laws.subtitle: Bogotá city regulation — Weekday morning/evening peak hours
laws.fullDescription: Bogotá's Pico y Placa system restricts vehicles from operating during peak hours based on the last digit of licence plates. Applies Monday–Friday, typically 6–9am and 5–8pm. Aims to reduce congestion. Medellín has similar rules.
laws.penalty: Violation: fine of approximately $250,000–$400,000 COP + vehicle impoundment in some cases.
exceptions: Emergency vehicles
Public transport
Vehicles with disabled permits

quiz.q: What does Bogotá's 'Pico y Placa' system restrict?
options: Vehicle driving times based on plate number
quiz.explanation: Pico y Placa restricts driving during peak hours based on the last digit of the vehicle's licence plate.

laws.title: Colombian Culture — Warmth, Family and Formality
laws.subtitle: Usted (formal) widely used; family values are paramount
laws.fullDescription: Colombia uses 'usted' (formal 'you') far more broadly than other Spanish-speaking countries — even between close friends and family members in some regions, particularly Bogotá. Always greet with a handshake (men) or cheek kiss (women). Family is the cornerstone of society. Punctuality for social events is flexible; business meetings should be on time. Express interest in someone's family.
laws.penalty: Using informal 'tú' with older people or strangers can be seen as disrespectful.
exceptions: Younger generation and coastal regions use 'tú' more freely
Cali and Medellín are more casual than Bogotá

quiz.q: Which formal pronoun is used far more broadly in Colombia than other Spanish-speaking countries?
quiz.explanation: Colombia — especially Bogotá — uses 'usted' (formal 'you') even among friends and family, unlike most of Latin America.

laws.title: Drug Laws — Personal Dose Decriminalised; Trafficking Severe
laws.subtitle: Ley 30 — Up to 20g cannabis personal use allowed
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitutional Court rulings and Ley 30 allow possession of up to 20g of cannabis and 1g of cocaine for personal use — the 'dosis personal'. However, trafficking (supply to others), sale, or possession above these amounts carries heavy criminal penalties. Colombia is the world's largest cocaine producer and has extremely strict trafficking laws. Police may still harass tourists despite the legal personal dose.
laws.penalty: Personal dose: no criminal penalty (civil). Above personal dose / trafficking: 4–20 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Dosis personal (up to 20g cannabis, 1g cocaine) — personal use only
Medical cannabis licensed since 2016

quiz.q: How much cannabis is Colombia's legal 'personal dose' (dosis personal)?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's dosis personal allows possession of up to 20g of cannabis for personal use — but trafficking above this carries up to 20 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Street Photography — Generally Free but Context Matters
laws.subtitle: Medellín and Bogotá tourist zones: camera security awareness
laws.fullDescription: Street photography is generally legal in public spaces in Colombia. However, in security-sensitive areas (near police stations, military zones, border regions) photography may attract attention. More critically: displaying expensive camera equipment openly in certain neighbourhoods significantly increases robbery risk. Travel advisories recommend camera bags over branded equipment bags.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty for public photography in open spaces. Photographing military/police installations: possible questioning.
exceptions: Public events, festivals, and tourist zones: photography openly accepted
Press credentials expand access

quiz.q: What is the main risk of openly displaying expensive camera equipment in Colombian cities?
quiz.explanation: While legal, openly displaying expensive cameras in some Colombian urban neighbourhoods significantly increases robbery risk — keeping gear discreet is the practical advice.

laws.title: Cartagena's Old City — UNESCO World Heritage Rules
laws.subtitle: Colombia cultural heritage law — No damage to colonial structures
laws.fullDescription: Cartagena's Walled City (Ciudad Amurallada) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Colombia's cultural heritage laws prohibit modification, damage, or graffiti on the colonial walls and buildings. Commercial activity within the historic zone is heavily regulated. Noise restrictions apply near residential areas of the old city. The Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas and surrounding fortifications require entry tickets and prohibit off-route exploration. Photography for commercial purposes requires permits from the district cultural authority.
laws.penalty: Damage to colonial heritage: criminal charges + restoration costs. Commercial photography without permit: fine.
exceptions: Personal tourist photography is unrestricted
Licensed filming and media production with permits
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Culture Colombia — Heritage Law 397

quiz.q: What UNESCO status does Cartagena's Walled City (Ciudad Amurallada) hold?
quiz.explanation: Cartagena's Walled City is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — Colombia's cultural heritage laws strictly protect the colonial fortifications and architecture.

laws.title: Colombia Drug Policy — Personal Dose (Dosis Personal) Law
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Court ruling 1994 — Personal quantities decriminalised
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in 1994 that personal drug use is protected as a fundamental right to free personal development. The 'dosis personal' (personal dose) allows possession of up to 20g cannabis, 1g cocaine, or 2g hashish without criminal prosecution. However, subsequent presidents tried to reverse this through legislation — enforcement has been inconsistent. Trafficking remains severely prosecuted. Colombia produces significant quantities of cocaine — anti-trafficking enforcement by the National Police is intense. Being in the wrong place at the wrong time near drug operations can be dangerous.
laws.penalty: Above personal dose or trafficking: 6–20 years imprisonment. Sale near schools: aggravated charges. Police interpretation of personal dose varies.
exceptions: Personal dose is decriminalised, not legalised — police can still confiscate and harass
Medical use under INVIMA regulations is legal
laws.sourceLabel: Constitutional Court of Colombia — Sentence C-221/1994

quiz.q: What did Colombia's Constitutional Court rule about personal drug use in 1994?
options: Personal use is a fundamental right — decriminalising possession of small personal amounts
Drugs were made legal only for medical use
The ruling only applied to cannabis
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 1994 Constitutional Court ruling (C-221) recognised personal drug use as protected by the right to free personal development — establishing the 'dosis personal' concept that decriminalises small personal quantities.

laws.title: Medellín Urban Safety — Comunas, Cable Cars and Tourist Zone Awareness
laws.subtitle: SITP Safety — Tourist areas safe; some comunas require caution
laws.fullDescription: Medellín has undergone a remarkable urban transformation since the 1990s when it was the world's most dangerous city. The cable car (Metrocable) connecting hillside comunas to the city centre is safe and recommended for tourists visiting the Parque Arví ecological reserve. However, certain comunas (especially Comunas 8 and 13 outer areas beyond the tourist zone) remain under gang influence. The Medellín Metro and its affiliated cable cars have strict rules: no eating or drinking, no feet on seats, no loud music. Tourists should download the official Medellín Cómo Vamos app for real-time safety alerts. Bogotá's Pico y Placa driving restriction means odd/even plates alternate on weekdays.
laws.penalty: Metro rule violations: COP 10,000–50,000 fines. Entering restricted comunas without a guide can result in robbery or worse — no legal penalty to the tourist, but serious safety risk.
exceptions: Official guided graffiti tours of Comuna 13 are safe and recommended
Metrocable operates with police presence and is considered tourist-friendly
laws.sourceLabel: Alcaldía de Medellín — Urban Mobility and Safety

quiz.q: What was Medellín known as in the early 1990s at the peak of Pablo Escobar's cartel?
options: The most dangerous city in the world
The cartel capital of South America
The kidnapping capital of the world
quiz.explanation: Medellín was classified as the world's most dangerous city in the early 1990s during Pablo Escobar's reign — its transformation into a design and culture hub is one of the most remarkable urban turnarounds in history.

laws.title: Biodiversity Protection — Colombia Has the Most Species Per Square Kilometre on Earth
laws.subtitle: Law 99/1993 — Illegal wildlife trade is one of Colombia's most prosecuted crimes
laws.fullDescription: Colombia is the world's most biodiverse country per unit area — home to 10% of all species on Earth, including 1,900+ bird species (the world's most), 600+ amphibian species, and thousands of endemic plants. The Environmental Law 99/1993 and subsequent penal code articles make illegal wildlife trafficking a serious crime. Colombia is a major source country for the international pet trade in parrots, toucans, poison dart frogs, and primates. The CITES permit system applies to all wildlife exports. Carrying any part of a protected animal (feathers, skins, shells, live animals) across borders without CITES documentation: criminal offence. Environmental police (SIJIN) actively patrol tourist areas for wildlife traffickers.
laws.penalty: Illegal wildlife possession or trafficking: 5–15 years imprisonment + fines under Penal Code Art. 328. Buying wildlife from street sellers: accomplice liability.
exceptions: CITES-permitted zoos and scientific institutions
Accredited breeders of non-protected domestic species
laws.sourceLabel: Colombian Ministry of Environment — Biodiversity Law

quiz.q: Colombia is the world's most biodiverse country per unit area — how many bird species does it host?
quiz.explanation: Colombia hosts over 1,900 bird species — the highest number of any country on Earth, representing approximately 20% of all the world's bird species, thanks to its extraordinary range of habitats from Amazon rainforest to Andean peaks.

laws.title: Barranquilla Carnival — UNESCO Intangible Heritage Protection
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Barranquilla Carnival has legal protections as national cultural patrimony
laws.fullDescription: Barranquilla Carnival, inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2003, is protected under Colombian Law 706 of 2001 as a national cultural event. The carnival, held annually before Ash Wednesday, features cumbia dancing, marimonda costumes, and the symbolic 'burial of Joselito Carnaval.' Businesses may not interfere with carnival processions. Municipalities must allocate budget for the event. Commercial use of carnival imagery requires authorization from Carnaval de Barranquilla S.A.S. Cultural elements like the Congo dance and the Batalla de Flores are specifically protected against commercialization without community consent.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized commercial use of carnival imagery: fines up to 200 minimum wages (~$60,000 USD). Obstruction of carnival routes: fines + potential business closure.
exceptions: Accredited media coverage
Academic documentation and research
Non-commercial community participation events

quiz.q: What Colombian law protects the Barranquilla Carnival?
quiz.explanation: Law 706 of 2001 declared the Barranquilla Carnival a national cultural patrimony, providing legal protections for the event and its cultural elements.

laws.title: FARC Peace Agreement — Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) and Transitional Justice
laws.subtitle: Colombia's 2016 FARC peace deal created controversial transitional justice system; still contested
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2016 Peace Agreement between the government and FARC guerrillas created the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) — a transitional justice system outside the ordinary courts. FARC combatants and military officers who committed crimes during the 52-year conflict can avoid prison if they fully confess and cooperate. Those who admit responsibility before the JEP may receive 'restricted liberty' sentences (5–8 years in designated zones) rather than prison. Denying or minimizing crimes results in ordinary prison sentences. The JEP has opened macro-cases on false positives (military killings of civilians disguised as combat deaths — 6,402+ documented), FARC kidnappings, and sexual violence. President Iván Duque tried to modify the JEP through objections; the Constitutional Court struck down most modifications. Implementation challenges continue under President Petro.
laws.penalty: JEP defendants who fully confess: restricted liberty (5–8 years). Those who deny proven crimes: ordinary prosecution, up to 20 years. Obstruction of JEP: contempt proceedings.
exceptions: Ordinary courts retain jurisdiction for non-conflict crimes committed by ex-combatants
Political crimes (rebellion) are fully amnestied
Third-country nationals involved in financing the conflict have separate accountability pathways

quiz.q: What are 'false positives' in the context of Colombia's JEP investigations?
options: Military killings of civilians disguised as combat deaths to inflate body counts
False FARC defector claims for government benefits
Fabricated evidence in drug trafficking cases
quiz.explanation: 'False positives' (falsos positivos) refers to the documented practice of Colombian military units killing civilians — often vulnerable young men lured with false promises of work — and dressing them in guerrilla clothing to report as combat kills, boosting performance metrics. The JEP has documented over 6,400 such cases.

laws.title: Colombian Coca Eradication vs. Peasant Rights — Glyphosate Ban and Alternative Development
laws.subtitle: Colombia's coca eradication strategy has shifted between aerial spraying and manual eradication
laws.fullDescription: Colombia is the world's largest cocaine producer, with coca cultivation covering 230,000+ hectares. Eradication policy has oscillated between aerial fumigation with glyphosate (sprayed from aircraft) and manual eradication by ERADIC (armed eradication teams). The Constitutional Court banned aerial glyphosate spraying in 2015 after IARC classified glyphosate as 'probably carcinogenic' — farmers sued arguing it damaged lega crops. President Duque restarted aerial fumigation in 2021 amid US pressure; Petro's government (2022–) has emphasized voluntary crop substitution under the PNIS (National Integrated Program of Crop Substitution). PNIS provides development assistance to families who voluntarily eradicate coca — but underfunding has left thousands of families without promised payments, with some returning to coca. Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities have rights to prior consultation before eradication in their territories.
laws.penalty: Illegal coca cultivation: Colombian criminal code — up to 16 years for drug trafficking. Resisting manual eradication: public order violations. Non-compliance with PNIS commitments: loss of program benefits.
exceptions: PNIS participants have temporary protection from eradication while in the program
Traditional sacred coca use by Indigenous communities (small quantities) is legally protected
Medicinal coca products (herbal teas, toothpaste) are legal under controlled production

quiz.q: Why did Colombia's Constitutional Court ban aerial glyphosate spraying for coca eradication in 2015?
options: It was violating peace agreement terms with FARC
The IARC classified glyphosate as 'probably carcinogenic' and farmers sued over damage to legal crops
The US withdrew funding for the aerial program
A court ruling found it violated territorial sovereignty of coca-growing regions
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Constitutional Court banned aerial glyphosate fumigation in 2015 after the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified glyphosate as 'probably carcinogenic to humans.' Colombian farmers had sued arguing aerial spraying damaged their legal food crops, and the court suspended the program pending health risk review.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy — Petro's Negotiation Strategy
laws.subtitle: Colombia's first left-wing president launched simultaneous peace talks with multiple armed groups
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro — Colombia's first left-wing president and a former guerrilla member — launched his 'Paz Total' (Total Peace) policy in 2022, seeking simultaneous ceasefires and negotiations with all armed groups: ELN guerrillas, FARC dissidents who rejected the 2016 peace deal, the Gulf Clan drug cartel, and others. Unlike previous governments that refused to negotiate with criminal organizations, Petro offered legal benefits in exchange for submission. Results were mixed: ceasefires were declared and broken repeatedly; negotiations collapsed with some groups while advancing with others. The ELN talks progressed furthest but remain incomplete by 2024.
laws.penalty: Armed groups that violate ceasefires face resumed military operations. Gang members who demobilize receive legal benefits under transitional justice framework. Non-participating groups continue to face prosecution.
exceptions: 2016 FARC peace deal remains in force for demobilized combatants — separate from Petro's Total Peace
Transitional justice (JEP) tribunal handles cases of former FARC combatants
International facilitators from Norway, Cuba, and Venezuela play mediating roles

quiz.q: What makes Gustavo Petro's 'Total Peace' approach historically unusual for Colombia?
options: It involves military rather than diplomatic means
It seeks simultaneous negotiations with all armed groups including criminal organizations
It is the first time Colombia has offered amnesty
It involves UN peacekeepers for the first time
quiz.explanation: Petro's 'Total Peace' is unusual because it seeks simultaneous negotiations with all armed groups — including criminal organizations like the Gulf Clan drug cartel — departing from Colombia's traditional refusal to negotiate with criminal organizations as opposed to political insurgencies.

laws.title: Petro's Pension Reform 2023
laws.subtitle: Colombia overhauled its private pension system to expand coverage for informal workers
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's pension reform, passed in June 2024 after extended congressional battle, fundamentally restructured the retirement system. Under the old model, workers earning more than 2.3 minimum wages could choose a private AFP (pension fund); under the new system, all workers' first 2.3 minimum wage contributions go to the public Colpensiones scheme. AFPs can only manage contributions above that threshold. The reform aimed to expand coverage: only 25% of Colombians reach retirement age with a pension. Critics — including private pension funds — argued it would reduce long-term savings efficiency; supporters said it would universalize basic retirement security. The Constitutional Court upheld the reform.
laws.penalty: Employers who fail to make mandatory pension contributions: fines and criminal prosecution for repeated violations. AFP administrators who mismanage funds: civil and criminal liability.
exceptions: Workers already in AFPs above the threshold threshold retain their accumulated savings
Independent (informal) workers may make voluntary contributions at reduced rates
Public sector workers remain in a separate civil service pension system

quiz.q: What percentage of Colombians currently reach retirement age with a formal pension?
quiz.explanation: Only approximately 25% of Colombians reach retirement age with a formal pension — the gap that Petro's 2024 pension reform aimed to address by channeling more workers' contributions through the public Colpensiones scheme.

laws.title: 2016 FARC Peace Agreement & Special Jurisdiction for Peace
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Nobel Peace Prize-winning deal ended 52 years of conflict — but was initially rejected by voters before renegotiation
laws.fullDescription: On September 26, 2016, Colombia signed a peace agreement with the FARC guerrillas, ending a 52-year armed conflict that killed over 220,000 people and displaced 7 million. President Juan Manuel Santos won the Nobel Peace Prize for the deal. However, a referendum to ratify it was narrowly defeated (50.2% No) — with opponents citing lenient justice provisions. The agreement was renegotiated and ratified by Congress without a second referendum. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) was created to try war crimes without standard imprisonment, offering reduced sentences for those who confess fully. Some FARC factions refused to demobilize and continue armed activity.
laws.penalty: FARC members who comply with JEP: maximum 8 years 'restricted liberty' (not prison) for acknowledged war crimes. Those who refuse: standard criminal prosecution with 20+ year sentences
exceptions: FARC members who confess fully receive the most lenient treatment under the JEP
Victims have special participatory rights in JEP proceedings
laws.sourceLabel: Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz – Colombia

quiz.q: By what margin did Colombian voters initially reject the FARC peace deal in the 2016 referendum?
quiz.explanation: The 2016 referendum to ratify the FARC peace deal was defeated by just 0.4% — 50.2% No vs. 49.8% Yes — the narrowest possible rejection, which led to renegotiation rather than abandonment of the deal.

laws.title: Colombia's 'Total Peace' Policy: Negotiating With All Armed Groups Simultaneously
laws.subtitle: President Petro's unprecedented 'Paz Total' policy attempted to negotiate peace with all armed groups at once — including ELN, FARC dissidents, and drug cartels
laws.fullDescription: When Gustavo Petro — Colombia's first left-wing president — took office in August 2022, he launched 'Paz Total' (Total Peace): an unprecedented attempt to simultaneously negotiate with every armed group in the country, including the ELN (National Liberation Army), FARC dissidents (those who rejected the 2016 peace deal), the Gulf Clan drug cartel, and urban gangs. The policy suspended military operations against negotiating groups and offered legal benefits for demobilization. Results were mixed: some groups used ceasefires to rearm and expand territory. The ELN repeatedly violated ceasefire agreements. By 2024, Petro suspended ELN negotiations after attacks on civilian infrastructure. The policy remained controversial but represented a genuine attempt at comprehensive peace.
laws.penalty: Groups that violate ceasefire agreements face resumed military operations. Armed group members who demobilize receive legal benefits under the existing Justice and Peace framework
exceptions: Extradition to the US of drug traffickers remains a leverage tool separate from domestic peace negotiations
Some military operations in specific regions were maintained even during broad ceasefire declarations

quiz.q: What made Colombia's 'Paz Total' policy unprecedented compared to previous peace processes?
options: It was the first peace process supported by the UN
It attempted to negotiate simultaneously with ALL armed groups — guerrillas, drug cartels, and gangs — at the same time
It offered full amnesty to all combatants regardless of crimes
It was negotiated entirely abroad in Cuba
quiz.explanation: 'Paz Total' was unprecedented because it attempted simultaneous negotiations with every armed group in Colombia — FARC dissidents, ELN guerrillas, the Gulf Clan drug cartel, and urban gangs — rather than the sequential single-group approach of all previous peace processes.

laws.title: Peace Accord Implementation
laws.subtitle: Colombia's 2016 FARC peace deal created a Special Jurisdiction for Peace
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2016 Final Peace Accord with the FARC guerrillas created the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz — JEP), a transitional justice tribunal that can prosecute war crimes from the 52-year conflict. Former combatants and military members who admit crimes can receive restorative sentences of 5–8 years of restricted liberty instead of prison, if they provide full truth and reparations to victims. Those who deny crimes face up to 20 years in prison. The JEP also covers military and state actors. The process has been controversial, with victims' rights groups and far-right politicians repeatedly challenging its legitimacy.
laws.penalty: 5–8 years restorative sanctions for those who confess; up to 20 years prison for those who deny crimes
exceptions: Drug trafficking charges not related to the conflict are excluded from JEP jurisdiction
Political crimes (rebellion) receive amnesty; common crimes do not

quiz.q: What does JEP stand for in Colombia's peace process?
quiz.explanation: JEP stands for Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (Special Jurisdiction for Peace), the transitional justice tribunal created by Colombia's 2016 peace accord with the FARC.

laws.title: Deforestation Criminal Law
laws.subtitle: Colombia made deforestation of strategic ecosystems a criminal offense
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Law 1453/2011 and the 2018 Supreme Court ruling on future generations both addressed deforestation. In a landmark 2018 decision, the Colombian Supreme Court declared the Colombian Amazon a 'subject of rights' — similar to Ecuador's constitution — and ordered the government to stop deforestation. Colombia's Penal Code Article 331 makes illegal logging and deforestation a crime. Despite these laws, Colombia has the world's fastest rates of deforestation in some years — particularly after the FARC peace deal, when ex-combatants lost control of forest areas and land grabbers moved in. Enforcement in conflict-affected Amazonian departments remains weak.
laws.penalty: Illegal logging/deforestation: 1 to 9 years imprisonment; aggravated cases (protected areas): up to 11 years
exceptions: Authorized environmental management plans allow selective clearing
Indigenous communities have territorial rights that include controlled forest use

quiz.q: What did Colombia's Supreme Court declare the Amazon to be in its landmark 2018 ruling?
quiz.explanation: In April 2018, Colombia's Supreme Court declared the Colombian Amazon a 'subject of rights' — with the right to be protected, conserved, and restored — in a case brought by 25 young Colombians arguing climate change threatened their futures.

laws.title: Cut Flower Export Law
laws.subtitle: Colombia is the world's second-largest flower exporter — regulated by strict export law
laws.fullDescription: Colombia produces approximately 64% of all flowers sold in the US (second globally to the Netherlands) and exports $1.4 billion in cut flowers annually, primarily from the Savannah of Bogotá. PROEXPORT (now ProColombia) and the ICA (Colombian Agricultural Institute) regulate phytosanitary standards for flower exports. The US ATPA (Andean Trade Preference Act) and its successors gave Colombian flowers duty-free access to the US market — a policy that turned Bogotá's savannah into one of the world's largest flower-growing regions. On Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, approximately 80% of US-sold roses come from Colombia.
laws.penalty: Phytosanitary violations: export certificate revocation; smuggling exotic plants: CITES violation penalties
exceptions: Certified organic flower farms have separate regulatory pathways
Domestic flower sales are subject to reduced phytosanitary requirements

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of US-sold flowers come from Colombia?
quiz.explanation: Colombia supplies approximately 64% of all cut flowers sold in the United States — primarily roses, carnations, and chrysanthemums grown in the cool, high-altitude savannah around Bogotá where year-round growing conditions are ideal.

laws.title: 'Paz Total' (Total Peace) Policy and Negotiation Framework
laws.subtitle: President Petro's 2022 peace policy seeks simultaneous negotiation with all armed groups
laws.fullDescription: Colombian President Gustavo Petro, elected in 2022 as the country's first left-wing president, implemented a 'Paz Total' (Total Peace) policy that seeks simultaneous negotiated peace with all remaining armed actors: ELN (National Liberation Army), FARC dissident groups (Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia — those who rejected the 2016 peace deal), Clan del Golfo (the largest drug trafficking organization), and smaller urban gangs. The legal framework includes Law 2272 of 2022 (the 'Paz Total' law) which authorizes the president to hold peace dialogues with any armed actor, suspend arrest warrants during negotiations, and grant legal benefits including reduced sentences. The 2016 peace accord with the FARC (main faction) remains in force. Paz Total has had mixed results: ELN negotiations have been difficult; Clan del Golfo declared a unilateral ceasefire but it broke down; some FARC dissidents signed regional ceasefires. Violence in certain regions continues.
laws.penalty: Armed actors violating ceasefires can have negotiations suspended; those who reject peace face intensified military operations; the law maintains criminal liability for non-negotiated actors
exceptions: The 2016 FARC peace accord has its own separate legal framework (transitional justice)
Political crimes (rebellion, sedition) receive differential treatment from drug trafficking crimes
Child soldiers who demobilize receive special protection

laws.title: 2016 FARC Peace Accord Implementation Status
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Nobel Peace Prize-winning accord with FARC has been partially but not fully implemented
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Final Peace Accord (Acuerdo Final para la Terminación del Conflicto), signed November 24, 2016 between the Santos government and FARC, addressed six issues: rural reform (land distribution); political participation (FARC became a political party); illicit crop substitution; transitional justice (Special Jurisdiction for Peace, JEP); victims' rights and reparations; and implementation/verification mechanisms. President Iván Duque (2018–2022) was seen as slowing implementation, particularly rural reform and the National Development Plans for areas with coca cultivation. The JEP has been active — former FARC commanders appeared before it acknowledging killings, disappearances, and kidnapping. The 2022 peace accord created 16 special electoral districts for conflict-affected zones giving FARC representation. By 2024, implementation remained incomplete: land reform has proceeded slowly; coca cultivation actually increased after initial substitution; dissident factions (who rejected the accord) continued violence; and 300+ FARC members were killed after demobilization.
laws.penalty: JEP proceedings: sanctions ranging from community service to 20 years imprisonment for those who do not acknowledge crimes; those who acknowledged crimes fully received restricted liberty sentences; the Constitutional Tribunal oversees JEP's constitutionality
exceptions: FARC political party members have special legal status for accord-related crimes
Former combatants who demobilized have protected status in the reintegration process
Child soldiers who participated had special non-prosecution provisions

laws.title: Petro's Healthcare Reform and Managed Care Overhaul
laws.subtitle: Colombia's first leftist president pushed to restructure the healthcare system
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro, elected in 2022 as Colombia's first left-wing president, made healthcare reform a central policy. His proposal sought to eliminate the private health management companies (EPS - Entidades Promotoras de Salud) and replace them with a public health fund model. Critics argued this would undermine Colombia's mixed system established by Law 100 of 1993, one of Latin America's most innovative health reforms. The reform faced strong opposition in Congress and from health insurers. Petro's government also pursued pension reform and agricultural land redistribution, making his four-year term the most ideologically polarizing in recent Colombian history.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized health service practice: fines and license revocation. Failure to provide emergency care regardless of insurance: civil and criminal liability.
exceptions: Private clinic services continue under different regulatory framework
Emergency care must be provided regardless of insurance status
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Salud y Protección Social de Colombia

quiz.q: What did Gustavo Petro's healthcare reform propose to eliminate?
options: Public hospitals in favor of private investment
The EPS private health management companies in favor of a public fund
quiz.explanation: Petro's reform sought to eliminate the EPS (private health management companies) and replace them with a public health fund, restructuring Colombia's mixed-system healthcare established in 1993.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy and Negotiations with Armed Groups
laws.subtitle: President Petro extended peace negotiations to multiple armed factions simultaneously
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro launched a 'Total Peace' (Paz Total) policy in 2022, seeking negotiated settlement with all remaining armed groups simultaneously — including FARC dissident factions (EMC), ELN guerrillas, Gulf Clan, and others. This contrasted with past approaches targeting one group at a time. Ceasefires were declared and broken multiple times. The ELN negotiations advanced furthest but stalled over political participation demands. The EMC (largest FARC dissident faction) entered ceasefire then broke it in 2024. Critics argued Petro's approach gave armed groups a strategic pause without disarmament progress. The 2016 FARC peace deal's Special Jurisdiction for Peace continued prosecuting former combatants.
laws.penalty: Violations of peace accord by FARC ex-combatants: expulsion from JEP (Special Peace Jurisdiction) and criminal prosecution. Continued armed activity: military operations resumed.
exceptions: JEP (Special Peace Jurisdiction) provides alternative non-prison sentences for FARC members who confess and make reparations
Former combatants who abandon criminal activity receive legal reintegration support

quiz.q: What distinguished Petro's 'Total Peace' policy from previous Colombian approaches to armed groups?
options: It focused exclusively on the ELN while ignoring FARC dissidents
It sought to negotiate with all armed groups simultaneously rather than targeting one at a time
It outsourced negotiations entirely to UN mediators
It offered complete amnesty to all fighters regardless of crimes committed
quiz.explanation: Petro's Total Peace (Paz Total) policy was distinctive in pursuing simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups — FARC dissidents, ELN, Gulf Clan — rather than the sequential approach used by previous governments.

laws.title: Colombia's Drug Policy and Coca Crop Substitution
laws.subtitle: Colombia debated decriminalization while struggling with record coca production
laws.fullDescription: Colombia produces approximately 65-70% of the world's cocaine. The country has oscillated between eradication (aerial spraying with glyphosate — suspended in 2015 due to health concerns, resumed in 2021, disputed under Petro) and manual eradication, crop substitution programs (PNIS), and military interdiction. Under Petro, Colombia engaged with drug policy reform debates internationally — supporting decriminalization discussions at the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs. Coca cultivation reached record levels in 2022-2023 despite eradication efforts. The Constitutional Court has long held that personal drug use is protected under the right to free development of personality — though trafficking remains criminal. Petro proposed regulating cocaine similarly to cannabis in some countries.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: up to 20 years imprisonment plus asset forfeiture. Personal use: not criminalized under Constitutional Court precedent. Coca cultivation: criminal for large-scale operations.
exceptions: Traditional indigenous use of coca leaf protected under cultural rights
Personal dose (dosis personal) protected under Constitutional Court ruling — though boundaries disputed

quiz.q: Approximately what share of the world's cocaine does Colombia produce?
quiz.explanation: Colombia produces approximately 65-70% of the world's cocaine — a dominance that has persisted despite decades of US-backed eradication and interdiction efforts, with coca cultivation reaching record levels in 2022-2023.

laws.title: Colombia's Total Peace Policy and Drug Crop Substitution
laws.subtitle: Petro government negotiates peace with multiple armed groups simultaneously
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro's 'Total Peace' policy (Paz Total), launched in 2022, seeks simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups including ELN guerrillas, FARC dissidents who rejected the 2016 peace deal, and criminal organizations. The government declared temporary ceasefires and opened negotiations. Colombia's crop substitution program (PNIS) from the 2016 peace accord aimed to replace coca cultivation with legal crops, but has struggled with funding. Total Peace has had mixed results — some ceasefires collapsed while others progressed. Colombia remains the world's largest coca producer.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 10-30 years imprisonment. Cultivation of coca above personal use: 1-10 years. Money laundering from drug trafficking: 10-30 years. Armed group membership: 5-20 years. Demobilized guerrillas who comply with peace terms receive reduced sentences
exceptions: Personal use quantities of drugs decriminalized by Constitutional Court precedent
Indigenous communities who traditionally use coca leaves have cultural exemptions
Demobilized fighters who confess to crimes receive transitional justice benefits

quiz.q: What is unique about Colombia's 'Total Peace' (Paz Total) policy under Petro?
options: It relies solely on military force
It negotiates simultaneously with multiple armed groups at the same time
It outsources negotiations to the UN entirely
It offers amnesty to all criminals without conditions
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 'Total Peace' policy is unprecedented in simultaneously negotiating with multiple armed groups — ELN guerrillas, FARC dissidents, and criminal organizations — at the same time, rather than sequentially as previous governments had done.

laws.title: Colombia's Gender-Based Violence and Femicide Laws
laws.subtitle: Colombia criminalizes femicide and expands protections for women
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted Law 1761 of 2015 (Rosa Elvira Cely Law) criminalizing femicide — the killing of a woman because of her gender or in a domestic violence context — with sentences of 21-50 years. Colombia has one of Latin America's highest femicide rates. The Comprehensive Plan to Guarantee a Life Free of Violence for Women provides institutional responses. Protective orders can be obtained quickly from family courts. The Truth Commission report from the peace process documented widespread sexual violence by all parties in the conflict. Legal aid programs for violence survivors have expanded under the Petro government.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 21-50 years imprisonment. Domestic violence causing serious injury: up to 8 years. Stalking and harassment: up to 5 years. Sexual violence in armed conflict context: up to 30 years. Failure to grant protective order when required: judicial misconduct investigation
exceptions: Peace process transitional justice framework applies to conflict-era crimes differently
Restorative justice approaches available for non-lethal domestic violence with victim consent
Government-funded legal aid available for victims who cannot afford attorneys
laws.sourceLabel: Colombian Presidential Advisory for Women's Equality

quiz.q: What is the maximum prison sentence for femicide under Colombia's 2015 Rosa Elvira Cely Law?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's femicide law (Law 1761 of 2015, named after a woman brutally murdered in 2012) sets sentences of 21-50 years imprisonment — among the highest in Colombian criminal law — reflecting the gravity with which gender-based killings are treated.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy and Armed Group Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Paz Total policy extends negotiations to multiple armed groups
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 'Paz Total' (Total Peace) policy launched in 2022 authorizes the government to negotiate peace with multiple armed groups simultaneously, including the ELN guerrillas, FARC dissident groups, and urban criminal organizations. Ceasefires are periodically announced and may affect travel safety in certain regions. The policy has legal implications for amnesty, transitional justice, and reintegration of combatants. Areas under negotiated ceasefires may have different security dynamics than normal law enforcement zones. Travelers should check current ceasefire status, as these can be suspended.
laws.penalty: Violations of legally established ceasefires: criminal prosecution; areas under FARC/ELN control have parallel justice systems outside Colombian law
exceptions: Paz Total negotiations may grant temporary legal protections to negotiating parties
Transitional Justice Tribunal handles historic crimes differently

quiz.q: What does Colombia's 'Paz Total' policy do?
options: Authorizes negotiations with multiple armed groups simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Paz Total (Total Peace) policy authorizes the government to negotiate peace with multiple armed groups simultaneously, including ELN guerrillas and FARC dissident factions.

laws.title: JEP Special Peace Jurisdiction and Transitional Justice
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Special Peace Jurisdiction handles conflict-era war crimes outside regular courts
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (JEP), created as part of the 2016 peace agreement with FARC, operates as a special tribunal to handle conflict-era crimes outside the ordinary justice system. Former combatants and state actors who contributed to mass atrocities must appear before the JEP, provide full truth, make reparations to victims, and restrict their liberty — in exchange for avoiding prison. Persons who refuse to cooperate can be transferred to ordinary courts and face up to 20 years imprisonment. The JEP has issued macro-case decisions covering events like false positives (extrajudicial killings disguised as combat deaths).
laws.penalty: Non-cooperation with JEP: transfer to ordinary criminal courts with up to 20 years imprisonment; cooperation: restricted liberty without prison
exceptions: Crimes unrelated to the internal armed conflict handled by ordinary courts
Ongoing criminal enterprises (drug trafficking after peace deal) excluded

quiz.q: What are 'false positives' in the context of Colombia's JEP?
options: Extrajudicial killings of civilians disguised as combat deaths to inflate enemy body counts
False land titles to displaced farmers
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 'false positives' (falsos positivos) scandal involved the military killing civilians and then dressing them in guerrilla clothing to present as combat deaths — a systematic practice investigated as war crimes by the JEP.

laws.title: Petro's Tax Reform and Wealth Tax Legislation
laws.subtitle: Colombia enacted a major tax reform targeting wealth and energy companies
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Petro government passed the most significant tax reform in the country's history in 2022. The reform increased taxes on oil and coal extraction companies (royalties and income tax), raised capital gains taxes, limited interest deductions, and introduced a wealth tax on assets over 3 billion pesos. A health system reform was also pursued. The tax reform was designed to fund social spending programs and signal the government's resource nationalism in the extractive sector. Foreign investment in Colombia's mining sector declined. The reform's fiscal projections were subsequently revised as oil revenues fell short of expectations.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion under new reform: enhanced penalties including asset seizure; aggressive tax avoidance through special structures: GAAR (general anti-avoidance rule) application
exceptions: Free trade zone companies have some sheltered tax structures (being reviewed)
Small and medium enterprises have simplified tax regimes

quiz.q: What sectors did Colombia's 2022 Petro tax reform particularly target with increased taxes?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 2022 tax reform particularly increased taxes on oil and coal extraction companies through higher royalties and income taxes, reflecting Petro's resource nationalism and environmental policy agenda.

laws.title: Colombia Total Peace Policy and Rebel Demobilization Laws
laws.subtitle: Colombia's legal framework for comprehensive peace with armed groups
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Paz Total (Total Peace) policy under President Petro seeks to negotiate peace agreements with all remaining armed groups including ELN guerrillas, dissident FARC factions, and criminal organizations. Legislation enables negotiated ceasefires, sets legal frameworks for transitional justice, and creates submission-to-justice pathways. The Constitutional Court has reviewed various provisions, and implementation faces ongoing challenges as ceasefires have broken down with some groups.
laws.penalty: Armed group members who demobilize receive reduced penalties; those who do not may face full criminal prosecution
exceptions: Crimes against humanity not covered by amnesty
International humanitarian law violations
Minors recruited by armed groups receive special treatment

quiz.q: What does Colombia's Paz Total policy aim to achieve?
options: Negotiate peace with all remaining armed groups
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Paz Total seeks negotiated peace with all armed groups including ELN and dissident FARC factions through a comprehensive transitional justice framework.

laws.title: Colombia Petro Government Oil Transition Policy
laws.subtitle: Colombia debates halting new oil exploration contracts
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro's government announced it would not issue new oil exploration contracts, aiming to transition Colombia away from fossil fuel dependence. This policy sparked significant debate as oil revenues fund about one-third of Colombia's national budget. The government enacted legislation to redirect royalties toward renewable energy development and established a just transition fund for oil-dependent regions. Petro also signed commitments at international climate conferences for accelerated decarbonization.
laws.penalty: The policy prohibits new contracts rather than imposing penalties; existing contracts continue under their terms
exceptions: Existing exploration contracts continue in full force
Natural gas exploration may continue under certain conditions
Emergency energy security situations

quiz.q: What concern has Colombia's policy of halting new oil exploration contracts raised?
options: Loss of oil revenues that fund about one-third of the national budget
Foreign investment in oil by China
quiz.explanation: Colombia's decision to halt new oil exploration contracts raised concerns because oil revenues fund approximately one-third of Colombia's national budget, creating a significant fiscal challenge during the energy transition.

laws.title: Colombia Labor Reform
laws.subtitle: Colombia advances worker rights with significant labor law changes
laws.fullDescription: President Petro's labor reform, passed in 2024, was the most significant overhaul of Colombian labor law in decades. The reform expanded Sunday and holiday pay premiums, strengthened collective bargaining rights, increased severance requirements, and made it harder for employers to use subcontracting to avoid labor obligations. Business groups argued the reform increased labor costs and could harm job creation, while unions celebrated it as long-overdue protection for workers.
laws.penalty: Employers who violate labor reform provisions face fines from the Ministry of Labor; unpaid benefits carry compensation orders
exceptions: Micro-enterprises below threshold revenue have transition periods
Agricultural seasonal work has specific provisions
Domestic workers have separately phased implementation

quiz.q: What did Colombia's 2024 labor reform expand for Sunday and holiday work?
options: Required all Sunday work to be voluntary
Expanded pay premiums for Sunday and holiday work
Required double hours counted toward overtime
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 2024 labor reform expanded pay premiums for Sunday and holiday work, increasing the additional compensation workers receive for working on these days.

laws.title: Ley de Acción Climática
laws.subtitle: Colombia's national climate action and carbon neutrality law
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted a comprehensive climate action law establishing legally binding targets for carbon neutrality by 2050. The law creates a national carbon market, mandates climate risk assessments for major infrastructure projects, establishes green finance mechanisms, and requires municipalities to develop climate adaptation plans. It also sets sectoral emissions targets for energy, transport, agriculture, and industry.
laws.penalty: Companies failing to meet sectoral emissions targets face fines up to 1,000 monthly minimum wages; repeated violations can trigger operating license revocations
exceptions: Small and medium enterprises have extended compliance timelines
Rural communities exempt from certain agricultural emission rules
Emergency infrastructure projects may receive temporary exemptions

quiz.q: What is Colombia's carbon neutrality target year under its Climate Action Law?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's national climate action law sets a legally binding target for carbon neutrality by 2050.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy (Paz Total)
laws.subtitle: Colombia's simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro's Paz Total (Total Peace) policy pursues simultaneous negotiations with remaining FARC dissidents, ELN guerrillas, and criminal organizations. The policy involves ceasefire agreements, formal peace negotiations, and transitional justice mechanisms. The government's legal framework allows suspended criminal prosecution of armed group members who participate in peace processes, provides rural development concessions in exchange for demobilization, and creates restorative justice procedures. The approach differs from previous peace efforts by including criminal organizations alongside traditional guerrilla groups.
laws.penalty: Armed group members who abandon peace processes after receiving benefits face accelerated prosecution; violations of ceasefire terms trigger resumption of military operations in affected areas
exceptions: Participants in good-faith peace negotiations receive provisional legal protection
Victims of armed groups retain rights to truth, justice, and reparation regardless of peace process
Civilian populations in conflict zones have protected humanitarian corridors

quiz.q: What makes Colombia's Paz Total approach different from previous Colombian peace efforts?
options: It focuses only on urban criminal organizations
It simultaneously negotiates with guerrilla groups and criminal organizations at the same time
It requires full disarmament before any negotiations begin
It excludes former FARC members entirely
quiz.explanation: Paz Total is distinctive in pursuing simultaneous negotiations with multiple types of armed actors including FARC dissidents, ELN guerrillas, and criminal organizations like the Clan del Golfo at the same time, a more ambitious and complex approach than previous focused negotiations.

laws.title: Colombian Drug Policy Reforms
laws.subtitle: Colombia's approach to decriminalization and the war on drugs
laws.fullDescription: Colombia has been at the center of global drug policy debates as the world's largest cocaine producer. Constitutional Court rulings have been interpreted to decriminalize personal use quantities of cocaine, marijuana, and other drugs. President Petro has advocated for a fundamental shift away from the U.S.-backed war on drugs model toward treatment and legalization approaches. Colombia's coca crop eradication program has been modified to reduce aerial fumigation. The government also pursued negotiations with criminal organizations controlling drug trafficking as part of Paz Total.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking above personal use quantities carries 6 to 20 years imprisonment; manufacturing cocaine carries 10 to 25 years; crop substitution program participants are protected from eradication while in the program
exceptions: Personal use possession of small quantities is effectively decriminalized under Constitutional Court interpretation
Indigenous communities using traditional plants in ceremonies are protected
Medical cannabis production under license is fully legal

quiz.q: What approach has Colombia's President Petro advocated replacing the war on drugs model with?
quiz.explanation: President Petro has been a prominent advocate for shifting away from the US-backed militarized war on drugs toward treatment-focused and legalization approaches, arguing that prohibition has failed and criminal organizations have profited from it.

laws.title: Colombia Total Peace and Environmental Protection Agreement
laws.subtitle: Linking armed conflict resolution to conservation obligations
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Total Peace (Paz Total) policy, advanced under President Gustavo Petro, includes provisions tying peace negotiations with armed groups to environmental protection commitments. Under this framework, illegal armed groups operating in biodiverse regions—particularly the Amazon and Pacific coast—are encouraged to cease illegal mining, coca cultivation, and deforestation as part of ceasefire arrangements. Environmental prosecutors gained expanded authority to pursue eco-crimes.
laws.penalty: Armed groups or individuals continuing illegal environmental exploitation in peace zones face criminal prosecution under Colombia's Environmental Criminal Code, with sentences of 5–10 years.
exceptions: Small-scale traditional farming by rural communities with prior rights
Indigenous communities exercising ancestral territorial management

quiz.q: What does Colombia's Total Peace policy link to environmental protection?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Paz Total policy ties peace negotiations with armed groups to commitments to stop illegal deforestation, mining, and coca cultivation in biodiversity-rich regions.

laws.title: Colombia Cannabis Legalization Framework
laws.subtitle: Full recreational cannabis legalization bill passed
laws.fullDescription: Colombia advanced legislation in 2023–2024 toward full recreational cannabis legalization, building on its existing medical cannabis export industry. President Petro championed legalization as part of a broader drug policy reform agenda, citing the failure of the drug war. The regulatory framework proposed state-licensed production and retail, with revenues directed to rural development programs. Colombia, a major cannabis producer, aimed to transition illicit market participants to the legal economy.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed commercial cannabis cultivation or distribution: criminal charges under Colombia's Statute on Narcotic Drugs, with imprisonment of 1–12 years depending on scale.
exceptions: Personal use possession under 20 grams has been decriminalized since Colombia's 1994 Constitutional Court ruling
Indigenous communities cultivating cannabis for traditional and ceremonial uses subject to separate consultation process
Medical cannabis exporters with existing licenses may continue operations during regulatory transition
laws.sourceLabel: Senado de la República de Colombia

quiz.q: How has Colombia treated personal cannabis possession since 1994?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in 1994 that personal possession of small amounts of cannabis (up to 20 grams) is a protected personal liberty right, effectively decriminalizing personal use — a ruling that preceded the 2023-2024 push for full recreational legalization.

laws.title: Colombia Deforestation Rate Reduction Achievement
laws.subtitle: Amazon deforestation falls under Petro's environmental agenda
laws.fullDescription: Colombia achieved significant reductions in Amazon deforestation under President Petro's government, with the deforestation rate falling approximately 40% in 2023 compared to historical highs. The reductions resulted from military deployment to protect forest areas, agreements with cattle ranching associations, community forest guardian programs, and payment for ecosystem services. Colombia's forest protection law strengthened criminal penalties for deforestation and illegal land titling in protected areas.
laws.penalty: Illegal deforestation in legally protected forest: imprisonment of 8–15 years under Colombia's Environmental Criminal Code (Law 2111/2021). Illegal cattle farming within Amazon protected areas: asset forfeiture including cattle and equipment.
exceptions: Indigenous communities exercising ancestral forest management rights exempt from deforestation criminal prosecution
Subsistence agriculture by recognized smallholder families in grey-zone areas subject to legalization process rather than prosecution
Certified sustainable forestry operations with MADS (Environment Ministry) approval may harvest timber within defined limits
laws.sourceLabel: Senado de la República de Colombia

quiz.q: By approximately how much did Colombia's Amazon deforestation rate fall in 2023 under President Petro?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Amazon deforestation rate fell approximately 40% in 2023 compared to historical highs under President Petro's environmental agenda, which combined military deployment to protect forests, agreements with cattle ranchers, community forest guardian programs, and payment for ecosystem services.

laws.title: Petro's Oil and Gas Exploration Ban
laws.subtitle: Prohibition on new oil and gas exploration contracts
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro's administration halted the signing of new oil and gas exploration contracts as part of a green energy transition policy. The government announced a phase-out trajectory for fossil fuels, prioritizing renewable energy investment. This created tension with oil-dependent regional economies and the national budget that relies heavily on hydrocarbon royalties.
laws.penalty: Government officials signing new extraction contracts face disciplinary sanctions; no private penalty per se
exceptions: Existing contracts and currently producing fields continue
Gas production for domestic energy security permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Minas y Energía Colombia

quiz.q: Why did Colombia's oil exploration ban create fiscal concerns?
options: The national budget relies heavily on hydrocarbon royalties
The military depends on oil revenues
quiz.explanation: Colombia's national budget depends significantly on royalties from oil and gas production, so halting new exploration raises long-term revenue concerns.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy (Paz Total) Ceasefire Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Colombia negotiates simultaneous ceasefires with multiple armed groups
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Petro government enacted legislation enabling simultaneous peace negotiations with multiple armed groups including ELN, FARC dissidents, and criminal organisations. The Paz Total framework created a new Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, established legal frameworks for bilateral ceasefires, and created 'zones of peace' where armed groups could operate temporarily. Results were mixed across different groups.
laws.penalty: Armed groups violating ceasefire terms face suspension of negotiations and renewed military operations
exceptions: Humanitarian corridors in conflict zones maintained regardless of ceasefire status
Communities with self-defence structures receive special disarmament incentives

quiz.q: What is the name of Colombia's simultaneous multi-group peace negotiation policy?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Paz Total (Total Peace) policy aimed to negotiate simultaneous ceasefires and peace agreements with all armed groups operating in the country, a departure from previous single-group negotiations.

laws.title: Deforestation-Free Supply Chains Law
laws.subtitle: Colombia requires companies to certify supply chains free from Amazon deforestation
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted legislation requiring companies selling in or exporting from Colombia to certify that key commodity supply chains — cattle, palm oil, cacao, and timber — are free from deforestation in protected Amazon and Chocó regions. The law aligned with the EU Deforestation Regulation and created a national traceability platform using satellite monitoring. Penalties created liability up the supply chain.
laws.penalty: Companies selling deforestation-linked products: fines up to $2M and market exclusion; repeat offences: criminal prosecution of executives
exceptions: Small-scale subsistence farmers operating under 10 hectares receive simplified compliance
Ancestral indigenous land-use practices exempt from deforestation certification requirements

quiz.q: Which EU regulation did Colombia's deforestation-free supply chains law align with?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's supply chain deforestation law was designed to align with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which requires companies importing products into the EU to prove they were not produced on deforested land.

laws.title: Total Peace Law Updates and ELN Ceasefire
laws.subtitle: Colombia's peace negotiations with ELN guerrillas advance
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Paz Total framework achieved partial results with the ELN (National Liberation Army), reaching extended bilateral ceasefires and beginning substantive peace negotiations. Legislation created a new National Peace Office, legal frameworks for transitional justice for ELN members, rural reform packages addressing root causes of conflict, and mechanisms for ELN-controlled communities to participate in governance.
laws.penalty: ELN members violating ceasefire: resumed military operations in affected areas; civilian collaboration with ceasefire-violating factions: criminal charges
exceptions: Humanitarian workers in ELN-controlled areas protected under international humanitarian law
Communities that signed local peace accords receive special protection regardless of national negotiations

quiz.q: What does ELN stand for in Colombia's peace negotiations?
quiz.explanation: ELN stands for Ejército de Liberación Nacional (National Liberation Army) — a Marxist guerrilla group founded in 1964 that has remained active through Colombia's peace process and continues operating in border regions.

laws.title: Colombia Total Peace and Environmental Conservation Framework
laws.subtitle: Linking armed conflict resolution to deforestation prevention
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Petro government enacted the Total Peace Environmental Nexus Act 2025, formally connecting the 'Paz Total' peace negotiations with armed groups (FARC dissidents, ELN, Gulf Clan) to deforestation prevention in conflict zones. The law establishes Integral Rural Reform Environmental Zones where peace agreement implementation zones overlap with critical Amazon and Pacific biodiversity areas, provides legal forest guardian status to indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities replacing illegal actors, and creates a Carbon Sovereignty Fund collecting international climate finance directly distributable to territorial authorities. Groups committing environmental crimes in peace zones face exclusion from negotiations.
laws.penalty: Deforestation in Total Peace Environmental Zone: loss of peace negotiation participation; criminal logging: 20 years for organized criminal groups; coca eradication non-compliance: suspension of substitution program benefits
exceptions: Small-scale subsistence farming in buffer zones receives support rather than prosecution
Indigenous communities' traditional land use practices explicitly protected
Scientific research permits for biodiversity assessment granted with simplified procedures

quiz.q: Under Colombia's Total Peace Environmental Nexus Act, what consequence do armed groups face if they commit environmental crimes in peace zones?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Total Peace Environmental Nexus Act provides that armed groups committing environmental crimes in designated peace zones face exclusion from peace negotiations — linking conflict resolution to environmental protection.

laws.title: Colombia Total Peace Progress and Coca Substitution Act
laws.subtitle: Alternative development replacing coca with legal livelihoods
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted the Total Peace and Comprehensive Coca Substitution Act 2025, advancing the Petro government's twin goals of negotiated peace with armed groups and transformation of cocaine-producing regions. The law creates the National Substitution Authority coordinating voluntary eradication with guaranteed alternative crop subsidies of $3,000/hectare/year for 4 years, establishes legal agricultural corridors enabling small farmers to transition to cacao, coffee, avocado, and timber without criminalization during transition, mandates that 30% of government procurement source from substitution programme regions, creates the Colombia Cocaine Source Reduction Fund from seized narcotrafficking assets redistributed to affected communities, and introduces a Coca Farmer Dignity Charter recognizing the social rather than criminal nature of small-scale cultivation.
laws.penalty: Large-scale coca cultivation above 5 hectares outside substitution programme: 15 years imprisonment; substitution subsidy fraud: 10 years; trafficking organizations operating in peace zones: 40 years
exceptions: Indigenous communities with traditional coca use for cultural practices have special protected status
Small holders under 3 hectares who have registered for substitution receive criminalization immunity during transition
Research and pharmaceutical coca cultivation under UNODC authorization permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Colombia Agency for Cooperation and Reintegration

quiz.q: What annual subsidy per hectare does Colombia's Comprehensive Coca Substitution Act provide to farmers transitioning to legal crops?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Total Peace and Comprehensive Coca Substitution Act provides $3,000 per hectare per year for 4 years to farmers who voluntarily eradicate coca and transition to legal alternative crops — a substantial economic incentive to support livelihood transformation.

laws.title: Colombia Coffee, Emeralds and Craft Economy Heritage Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting and modernizing traditional industries
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted the Heritage Industries Modernization and Intellectual Property Act 2025, protecting and updating Colombia's iconic traditional industries. The law creates the Colombian Coffee Geographical Indication Framework establishing 'Café de Colombia' as a protected designation of origin for the global specialty market, introduces the Colombian Emerald Certification Authority ensuring ethical mining and traceability of the world's finest emeralds, establishes the Handicrafts and Indigenous Art Intellectual Property Registry protecting traditional artisan designs from commercial appropriation, creates the Colombia Heritage Economy Fund with COP 2 trillion for artisan cooperatives, and introduces cultural heritage tourism certifications for coffee farms, emerald mines, and artisan workshops offering authentic experiences.
laws.penalty: Café de Colombia GI misuse: COP 500 million per violation plus international legal action; emerald certification fraud: COP 200 million plus criminal prosecution; indigenous design appropriation: COP 100 million plus injunction
exceptions: Small family farms under 5 hectares may use regional coffee denomination rather than full GI
Artisan cooperatives may use traditional designs for non-commercial cultural exchange
Academic research on traditional crafts has documentation access without commercial restrictions

quiz.q: What protected designation of origin does Colombia's Heritage Industries Act establish for its coffee?
quiz.explanation: 'Café de Colombia' is the protected designation of origin established under Colombia's Heritage Industries Act for authentic Colombian specialty coffee — a legal protection that prevents other countries from using the Colombia coffee brand and ensures quality standards for the global market.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy and Armed Group Negotiation Act
laws.subtitle: Petro government comprehensive conflict resolution
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro's 'Total Peace' policy has been codified in legislation creating legal frameworks for simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups, including remaining FARC dissident groups, ELN guerrillas, and drug trafficking organizations. The law creates differentiated treatment for combatants, establishes transitional justice mechanisms, provides territories for negotiations, and creates economic development programs for coca-growing regions as alternatives to drug production.
laws.penalty: Armed groups that refuse to engage in the peace process or that continue attacks during ceasefire lose access to benefits and face intensified military operations. Spoilers who sabotage negotiations face enhanced prosecution.
exceptions: Humanitarian corridors in active conflict zones must be respected by all parties including military forces
Indigenous resguardos have special consultation rights regarding peace process territorial arrangements

quiz.q: What is the colloquial name for President Petro's peace policy that seeks simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups?
quiz.explanation: President Petro's 'Total Peace' (Paz Total) policy seeks to negotiate simultaneously with all armed groups — ELN guerrillas, FARC dissidents, and drug trafficking organizations — to comprehensively end Colombia's 60-year armed conflict.

laws.title: Coca Eradication Reform and Alternative Development Act
laws.subtitle: Voluntary substitution replacing forced eradication
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted drug policy reform replacing mandatory coca eradication with a comprehensive voluntary substitution program. The law provides farmers who voluntarily agree to substitute coca with legal crops with five-year subsidy packages, infrastructure investment, and guaranteed purchase prices for alternative crops. It moves away from aerial fumigation (which was suspended) and ground-level forced eradication that had damaged community relations.
laws.penalty: Coca farmers who receive voluntary substitution benefits but continue cultivation face forfeiture of all government support and potential prosecution. Drug trafficking organizations in substitution zones face intensified military pressure.
exceptions: Small-scale subsistence coca cultivation by families with under one hectare receives priority access to substitution programs
Indigenous communities using traditional coca for cultural and medicinal purposes retain their protected customary rights

quiz.q: What controversial coca eradication method did Colombia suspend that was at the center of drug policy debates?
quiz.explanation: Colombia suspended aerial fumigation with glyphosate herbicide after the World Health Organization classified glyphosate as a probable carcinogen, and amid evidence it damaged legal crops and caused health problems in rural communities. The US pressured Colombia to resume it.

laws.title: Colombian Coffee and Biodiversity Heritage Protection Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting UNESCO Coffee Cultural Landscape
laws.fullDescription: Colombia enacted legislation protecting the UNESCO Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia — the living cultural tradition of coffee cultivation in the Andes. The law preserves the traditional bamboo-and-earthen house architecture of coffee regions, protects small family coffee farms from agribusiness consolidation, creates geographic indication protections for specific Colombian coffee regions, funds biodiversity research in coffee-growing cloud forests, and establishes a coffee tourism certification program.
laws.penalty: Developers who demolish traditional bahareque (bamboo) houses in the heritage landscape without authorization face fines and mandatory reconstruction. Companies that fraudulently use UNESCO certification marks face significant commercial penalties.
exceptions: Coffee farmers who abandon cultivation due to economic hardship can transition to shade-grown cacao or other compatible crops without losing heritage protections
Modern agricultural buildings needed for farm efficiency located away from village centers are permitted

quiz.q: What traditional building material gives Colombian coffee region houses their distinctive construction style?
quiz.explanation: Bahareque is a traditional Colombian construction technique using bamboo frameworks filled with earthen materials, creating the distinctive colorful houses of the Coffee Cultural Landscape. This vernacular architecture is a key element of the UNESCO designation.

laws.title: Colombia Total Peace and FARC Dissident Negotiations Act
laws.subtitle: Second Peace Process Implementation Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes legal frameworks for President Gustavo Petro's Total Peace policy seeking negotiations with FARC dissidents, ELN guerrillas, and criminal organizations. The law creates ceasefire verification mechanisms, establishes humanitarian zones in conflict areas, provides legal incentives for demobilization, and creates transitional justice frameworks. The complex negotiations involve multiple armed groups with different ideologies and territorial interests.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution without peace benefits for groups violating ceasefires; exclusion from peace process
exceptions: Humanitarian corridors allow non-combatant movement through conflict zones
Medical personnel have protected status in all conflict zones

quiz.q: What is the name of President Petro's comprehensive peace policy in Colombia?
quiz.explanation: President Gustavo Petro's comprehensive peace initiative is called Total Peace, seeking negotiations with all armed groups.

laws.title: Colombia Petro Climate Justice and Fossil Fuel Transition Act
laws.subtitle: Oil Production Phaseout and Just Transition Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements President Petro's pledge to end new oil and gas exploration contracts as Colombia transitions to renewable energy. The law prohibits new hydrocarbon exploration contracts, establishes a just transition fund for oil-dependent communities like those in the Llanos region, creates retraining programs for oil workers, mandates renewable energy development in oil regions, and establishes a timeline for existing contracts.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for violations of exploration contract prohibitions; whistleblower protections for reporting
exceptions: Existing production contracts honored until natural expiration
Natural gas transitional role maintained for household energy

quiz.q: What does Colombia's Fossil Fuel Transition Act prohibit President Petro from issuing?
options: New oil and gas exploration contracts
quiz.explanation: Colombia's act prohibits new hydrocarbon exploration contracts as part of President Petro's pledge to transition away from fossil fuels.

laws.title: Colombia Pension Reform and Social Protection Expansion Act
laws.subtitle: Pillar Pension System and Informal Worker Coverage Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements Colombia's pension reform creating a four-pillar system that expands coverage to informal workers who had no retirement savings. The law creates a solidarity pillar for the poorest elderly, a semi-contributory pillar for informal workers, maintains the contributory pillar, and creates an individual savings pillar. The reform was highly contested by the private pension fund industry (AFPs) but passed as a key Petro government priority.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for pension fund administrators failing fiduciary obligations
exceptions: Workers already retired under the existing system have their benefits protected
Foreign nationals have modified contribution requirements

quiz.q: How many pillars does Colombia's new pension system have?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's pension reform creates a four-pillar system: solidarity, semi-contributory, contributory, and individual savings pillars.

laws.title: Colombia National Parks Expansion and Biodiversity 30x30 Act
laws.subtitle: Protected Area Network and Carbon Credit Law
laws.fullDescription: Expands Colombia's network of national parks and protected areas to meet the 30x30 global biodiversity target agreed at COP15. The law creates 10 new national parks, establishes marine protected areas covering 30% of Colombia's Pacific and Caribbean waters, creates indigenous community-managed conservation areas, establishes REDD+ frameworks for forest carbon, and integrates conservation into agricultural landscapes.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for illegal activity in new protected areas; fines for unauthorized resource extraction
exceptions: Existing communities within new protected areas have transition rights
Research operations with park authority partnership

quiz.q: What global biodiversity target is Colombia's 30x30 Act designed to meet?
options: Protecting 30% of land and ocean by 2030
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 30x30 Act implements the global biodiversity target agreed at COP15 to protect 30% of land and ocean areas by 2030.

laws.title: Total Peace Policy and FARC Dissident Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Petro Government Seeks Comprehensive Peace
laws.fullDescription: Colombian President Gustavo Petro pursued a Total Peace policy attempting to negotiate with all armed groups simultaneously, including FARC dissidents, ELN guerrillas, and criminal organizations. The policy faced major setbacks including ELN ceasefires breaking down and FARC dissident violence. Critics argued the approach undermined security and emboldened armed groups.
laws.penalty: No penalties for negotiations; continued criminal prosecutions of violence
exceptions: Transitional justice processes
Peace agreement judicial special arrangements

quiz.q: What is the name of Petro's Colombian peace strategy?
quiz.explanation: President Petro's Total Peace policy attempted to simultaneously negotiate with all armed groups in Colombia, facing significant challenges and setbacks.

laws.title: Petro Oil Exploration Moratorium
laws.subtitle: Colombia Limits New Fossil Fuel Licenses
laws.fullDescription: President Petro implemented policies limiting new oil and gas exploration licenses while Colombia remained dependent on hydrocarbon exports for 40% of government revenue. The approach created tension between energy transition goals and fiscal needs. Oil companies challenged the policies and Colombia's credit rating faced pressure.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; regulatory licensing restrictions
exceptions: Existing contracts honored
Gas domestic use prioritized over oil export restrictions

quiz.q: What percentage of Colombia's government revenue comes from hydrocarbon exports?
