quiz.explanation: Hydrocarbons provide approximately 40% of Colombia's government revenue, creating tension between Petro's energy transition goals and fiscal necessity.

laws.title: Drug Policy Reform and Coca Crop Substitution
laws.subtitle: Colombia Pursues Comprehensive Drug Policy Change
laws.fullDescription: Colombia under President Petro pursued a significant shift in drug policy away from eradication-focused approaches toward crop substitution, treatment, and harm reduction. The government proposed reducing cocaine criminalization domestically and sought to change international drug conventions. Relations with US counternarcotics programs were strained.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for trafficking maintained; possession decriminalization expanded
exceptions: US counternarcotics cooperation requirements
Coca crop substitution program voluntary

quiz.q: What approach did Colombia shift toward under Petro's drug policy?
options: Crop substitution, treatment, and harm reduction over eradication
quiz.explanation: Colombia shifted drug policy toward crop substitution, treatment, and harm reduction under Petro, moving away from eradication-focused approaches.

laws.title: Coffee Industry and Climate Adaptation
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Famous Coffee Faces Climate Pressure
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's world-famous coffee regions faced significant climate pressure with changing rainfall patterns, temperature increases, and new pests threatening traditional Arabica growing zones. Coffee farmers moved to higher altitudes and adopted new varieties. Colombia's coffee industry invested in climate-smart agriculture research.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; certification compliance for specialty coffee
exceptions: Smallholder support programs
Certification body partnerships

quiz.q: What primary climate-driven adaptation are Colombian coffee farmers making?
options: Moving to higher altitudes as temperatures rise
quiz.explanation: Colombian coffee farmers are moving to higher altitudes as climate change raises temperatures in traditional growing zones, threatening the optimal conditions for Arabica coffee.

laws.title: Pacific Biodiversity and Marine Sanctuary
laws.subtitle: Colombia Expands Pacific Ocean Protections
laws.fullDescription: Colombia significantly expanded marine protected areas in the Pacific including the Malpelo and Gorgonas UNESCO sites, adding buffer zones and enforcement. The Humboldt Current upwelling made Colombian Pacific waters extraordinarily biodiverse. Colombia championed Pacific biodiversity through the Galapagos Corridor marine management.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for illegal fishing in MPAs
exceptions: Traditional artisanal fishing community rights
Scientific research permits

quiz.q: What oceanographic phenomenon makes Colombia's Pacific waters extraordinarily biodiverse?
quiz.explanation: The Humboldt Current upwelling in the Colombian Pacific brings cold nutrient-rich water to the surface, creating extraordinarily biodiverse marine ecosystems.

laws.title: Petro's Total Peace Policy and Armed Group Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Colombia attempts comprehensive peace with all armed groups simultaneously
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president and former M-19 guerrilla, pursued 'Total Peace' — simultaneous ceasefire and peace negotiations with ELN guerrillas, FARC dissident groups, and drug trafficking organizations. The approach broke from precedent by negotiating with criminal organizations alongside political guerrillas. Results have been mixed: some ceasefires held, others collapsed. The policy represents the most ambitious attempt to end Colombia's 60-year armed conflict since the 2016 FARC peace deal.
laws.penalty: Armed groups violating ceasefire terms return to 'active' status with full military pressure
exceptions: Humanitarian ceasefires allow food and medicine access in conflict zones regardless of negotiation status
Political prisoners receive separate amnesty procedures from combatant demobilization

laws.title: Coffee Crisis and Climate Adaptation
laws.subtitle: Colombia's iconic coffee faces existential threat from warming
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's coffee, known for its mild flavor from high-altitude growing regions, faces existential threat from climate change. Rising temperatures are pushing optimal growing altitude higher, reducing available land. La Niña and El Niño cycles create unpredictable rainfall. The Colombian Coffee Federation supports farmers in adapting through new varieties, shade-growing techniques, and altitude shifts. Colombian specialty coffee commands premium prices globally but the commodity market remains volatile.
laws.penalty: Coffee certification schemes require adherence to quality and sustainability standards
exceptions: Small-scale farmers under 2 hectares qualify for simplified certification
Organic transition periods allow time to achieve certification without losing premium access

laws.title: Flower Export Dominance and Cut Flower Industry
laws.subtitle: Colombia supplies 80% of US cut flowers from Bogotá's highlands
laws.fullDescription: Colombia is the world's second-largest cut flower exporter and supplies 80% of flowers sold in the United States. Bogotá's savanna — at 2,600m altitude with perfect temperatures and light — produces 1.6 billion flowers annually. Valentine's Day and Mother's Day trigger massive Colombian flower harvests. The industry employs 200,000+ workers, mostly women. Dutch flower auction houses (FloraHolland) set global prices. Environmental concerns include pesticide use and the massive water consumption of intensive flower cultivation.
laws.penalty: Pesticide use in flower cultivation must comply with export market requirements from US and EU
exceptions: Organic-certified flower farms have different pesticide allowances
Small family farms under threshold acreage have simplified compliance documentation

quiz.q: What percentage of US cut flowers come from Colombia?
quiz.explanation: Colombia supplies approximately 80% of cut flowers sold in the United States — roses, carnations, chrysanthemums — grown in the highland savanna around Bogotá where altitude and climate create perfect growing conditions.

laws.title: Petro Government and Total Peace Negotiations
laws.subtitle: Colombia's first left-wing president pursuing comprehensive peace
laws.fullDescription: Gustavo Petro, elected in 2022 as Colombia's first left-wing president (and a former M-19 guerrilla), has pursued a 'total peace' (paz total) strategy attempting simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups including the ELN guerrillas, dissident FARC factions that rejected the 2016 peace deal, and criminal organizations. The strategy has had mixed results — some ceasefires have held temporarily, others have collapsed amid continued violence. Petro has also pursued progressive social policies including land reform, environmental protection of the Amazon (Colombia lost significant Amazon forest under previous governments), universal healthcare expansion, and pension reform. His relations with the US have been strained over drug policy — Petro has called US drug prohibition a failed strategy and sought a different approach. Colombia remains the world's largest cocaine producer despite decades of counter-narcotics efforts. Petro's coalition politics have been turbulent, with multiple cabinet reshuffles.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking carries severe criminal penalties; armed group membership can lead to prosecution or benefits under peace negotiations depending on cooperation
exceptions: Peace process participants may receive special legal treatment including reduced sentences

quiz.q: What is 'paz total' (total peace) as pursued by President Petro?
options: A military strategy to defeat all armed groups
Simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups and criminal organizations
quiz.explanation: 'Paz total' is Petro's strategy of pursuing simultaneous negotiations with multiple armed groups — including ELN guerrillas, dissident FARC factions, and criminal organizations — rather than a sequential approach to peacemaking.

laws.title: Amazon Protection and Deforestation Zero Commitment
laws.subtitle: Colombia's ambitious commitment to halt Amazon forest loss
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Amazon region represents a critical part of the global climate system and extraordinary biodiversity. Despite being smaller than Brazil's Amazon, Colombian Amazon faces significant deforestation pressure from cattle ranching, coca cultivation, illegal mining, and land grabbing following the 2016 peace deal, which reduced FARC guerrilla control that had paradoxically limited deforestation in some areas. President Petro has made Amazon protection a centerpiece of his environmental agenda, committing to deforestation zero and participating actively in Amazon Summit initiatives. The 2023 Amazon Summit in Belem brought together eight Amazon countries to coordinate conservation. Colombia has developed innovative conservation finance mechanisms and works with indigenous communities who are the most effective forest protectors. Petro has also called for reducing coal and oil extraction, though Colombia remains an important fossil fuel producer.
laws.penalty: Deforestation violations carry criminal penalties; environmental crimes are increasingly prosecuted under strengthened legal frameworks
exceptions: Some legal agricultural land clearing in certain zones remains permitted under forest code provisions

quiz.q: What paradoxical effect did the 2016 peace deal with FARC guerrillas have on Colombian Amazon deforestation?
options: Peace reduced deforestation as farmers felt safer from guerrilla taxation
FARC had paradoxically limited deforestation in some areas under their control, so peace increased it
Peace enabled government to enforce environmental laws more effectively
The peace deal included specific deforestation reduction commitments from FARC
quiz.explanation: The 2016 FARC peace deal paradoxically increased deforestation in some Colombian Amazon areas — FARC had controlled and limited deforestation in territories under their influence, and their withdrawal created an opening for cattle ranchers and land grabbers.

laws.title: Petro's Anti-Oil Transition Policy
laws.subtitle: President's fossil fuel phase-out meets economic reality
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro declared Colombia would stop issuing new oil exploration contracts, aiming to transition the economy away from fossil fuels. However oil revenues fund roughly 10% of the national budget, creating enormous fiscal pressure. The policy has faced resistance from Congress, oil companies and oil-dependent regions. A compromise involving continued exploitation of existing fields while banning new contracts has emerged as the working policy.
laws.penalty: New oil exploration contracts prohibited; existing contracts honored under grandfathering provisions
exceptions: Natural gas exploration continues as a transition fuel
Existing productive oil fields may continue operations

quiz.q: What percentage of Colombia's national budget comes from oil revenues?
quiz.explanation: Oil revenues fund roughly 10% of Colombia's national budget, making President Petro's anti-oil policy extremely challenging economically.

laws.title: Petro Total Peace Process
laws.subtitle: Colombia attempts simultaneous peace negotiations with all armed groups
laws.fullDescription: President Gustavo Petro launched an ambitious Total Peace policy attempting to negotiate simultaneously with the ELN guerrillas, criminal organizations like Gulf Clan and FARC dissident groups. The approach was more complex than previous peace processes and faced repeated setbacks as various groups broke ceasefires. Critics accused Petro of being naive about the criminal motivations of some groups. Some negotiations produced partial results while others collapsed. Colombia's peace remains elusive despite years of effort.
laws.penalty: Armed groups that break ceasefires face resumed military operations; criminal organizations not eligible for political amnesty
exceptions: Political crimes under defined criteria eligible for amnesty
Truth commission process for former FARC combatants continued under previous accord

quiz.q: What is the name of President Petro's peace approach attempting simultaneous negotiations with all armed groups?
quiz.explanation: President Petro's Total Peace policy attempted to negotiate simultaneously with all armed groups including the ELN, Gulf Clan and FARC dissidents—an ambitious but frequently frustrated approach to Colombia's complex security situation.

laws.title: Medellín Urban Innovation Model
laws.subtitle: Former murder capital becomes global smart city example
laws.fullDescription: Medellín transformed from the world's most dangerous city in the 1990s to a globally recognized urban innovation model. The city deployed cable cars and outdoor escalators to connect hillside comunas to the city center, reducing inequality and crime. Smart city initiatives include digital mobility systems, sensor networks and open data platforms. The Medellín Innovation District hosts tech companies and co-working spaces. The city's turnaround has been studied worldwide as a model of urban transformation through infrastructure investment in marginalized areas.
laws.penalty: Smart city data collection subject to Colombian data protection regulations; community consent processes for surveillance infrastructure
exceptions: Public safety camera networks operate under separate law enforcement framework
Innovation district companies have startup-friendly regulatory environment

quiz.q: What unusual transport infrastructure did Medellín install to connect hillside slum communities to the city center?
quiz.explanation: Medellín installed cable cars and outdoor escalators to connect hillside comunas to the city center—unusual infrastructure that reduced travel time for poor residents, symbolized investment in marginalized areas and helped transform the former murder capital.

laws.title: Coffee and Coca Economy Balance
laws.subtitle: Colombia's legal and illegal agricultural exports intertwined
laws.fullDescription: Colombia remains the world's top producer of mild Arabica coffee and third overall. Coffee is deeply embedded in Colombian culture and identity, supporting over half a million farming families. However Colombia also remains the world's largest coca producer and cocaine supplier. The drug economy generates billions annually, distorts rural economies and funds armed groups. The Colombian government under Petro has pursued an anti-fumigation approach, preferring crop substitution—with limited results. The interplay between legal and illegal agriculture shapes Colombian rural economics.
laws.penalty: Coca cultivation subject to eradication and crop substitution programs; cocaine trafficking carries severe criminal penalties
exceptions: Traditional indigenous coca use recognized as cultural practice
Crop substitution program participants protected from immediate eradication

quiz.q: What type of coffee is Colombia the world's top producer of?
quiz.explanation: Colombia is the world's top producer of mild Arabica coffee—the variety prized for its smooth flavor used in specialty coffee—supporting over half a million farming families while the country simultaneously remains the world's largest coca and cocaine producer.

laws.title: Climate Action Law
laws.subtitle: Net Zero and Biodiversity Protection
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2021 Climate Action Law (Law 2169) established legally binding targets to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050 and reduce emissions 51% by 2030, one of the most ambitious NDCs in Latin America. The law creates a national climate change system and mandates climate risk assessments for all public investment. Colombia is mega-biodiverse — second only to Brazil — and faces deforestation in the Amazon, which the law addresses by tying deforestation reduction to climate goals. President Petro, elected 2022, pledged to halt new oil and gas contracts.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for companies exceeding sector emission caps; environmental impact liability
exceptions: Subsistence communities
Energy security exemptions during transition

laws.title: Colombia Universal Health Coverage Law
laws.subtitle: Landmark Right to Health
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Law 100 (1993) transformed Colombian healthcare by creating a contributory health system where workers pay into insurance funds (EPS) and a subsidized regime covers the poor. Colombia achieved near-universal health coverage. A landmark 2022 Constitutional Court ruling recognized health as a fundamental right. Colombia's health reform debates center on EPS (private health insurers) corruption — endemic overcharging and failure to provide services — leading to President Petro's push for direct public provision. Colombia's universal coverage coexists with deep inequality in service quality.
laws.penalty: EPS failures to provide services are actionable through tutela constitutional remedy; criminal liability for health fraud
exceptions: Pre-existing conditions covered (no exclusions under Colombian law)
Emergency care universally guaranteed regardless of insurance status

laws.title: Colombia Labor Code Reform and Social Progress
laws.subtitle: Workers' Rights in a Violent Context
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Labor Code (Código Sustantivo del Trabajo) governs employment relations, and President Petro's government proposed significant reforms including expanding collective bargaining rights, increasing overtime pay, and strengthening union protections. Colombia has one of Latin America's most difficult environments for labor organizers — over 3,000 trade unionists have been killed since the 1980s, the highest globally. Colombia has a significant informal economy (60%+ of workers), making labor law enforcement challenging. Petro's reforms sparked significant business opposition and National Strike (Paro Nacional) dynamics.
laws.penalty: Unfair dismissal: severance pay mandatory; union interference: criminal liability; minimum wage violations: administrative fines
exceptions: Informal workers largely outside formal labor law
Domestic workers have special protections under Law 1595

laws.title: Colombia Free Higher Education for the Poor
laws.subtitle: Ser Pilo Paga and Generación E
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Generación E program provides free university tuition for the poorest students (SISBEN IV levels 1-3) at public and participating private universities. Under President Santos, the 'Ser Pilo Paga' (Being Smart Pays) program sent poor students to elite private universities — controversial for enriching private institutions with public money. Colombia's universities have seen significant student protests for education funding. Colombia also implemented a comprehensive teacher reform and merit-based promotion system. Rural education remains severely underfunded, contributing to educational inequality between urban and rural Colombia.
laws.penalty: Education quality monitored by Ministry; universities must meet accreditation; Generación E scholarship recipients must maintain academic standards
exceptions: Private universities may participate in scholarship programs
Religious universities under separate agreement

laws.title: Venezuelan Migrant Temporary Protection Status
laws.subtitle: Colombia's unprecedented mass regularization of Venezuelans
laws.fullDescription: Colombia implemented Temporary Protection Status (Estatuto Temporal de Protección para Migrantes Venezolanos - ETPV) in 2021, offering a 10-year temporary protected status to approximately 1.8 million Venezuelans—the largest mass regularization in Latin American history. Colombia hosts the world's second-largest Venezuelan displaced population after Venezuela itself. The ETPV allows Venezuelans to work legally, access healthcare and education, and establish formal residency. Colombia receives support from UNHCR and World Bank for this unprecedented integration effort.
laws.penalty: Venezuelans not registering for ETPV remain undocumented and subject to deportation; employers exploiting undocumented Venezuelans face labor law penalties
exceptions: ETPV registration was time-limited (open period ended 2021)
Venezuelans with existing visas may continue under previous status
laws.sourceLabel: Colombia ETPV – Venezuelan Migrant Protection Status

quiz.q: Colombia's 2021 ETPV provided 10-year temporary protection status to approximately how many Venezuelan migrants?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Estatuto Temporal de Protección para Migrantes Venezolanos (ETPV) offered 10-year temporary protected status to approximately 1.8 million Venezuelans, the largest mass regularization of migrants in Latin American history.

laws.title: Drug Policy and Coca Eradication
laws.subtitle: Colombia's evolution from drug war to crop substitution
laws.fullDescription: Colombia, historically the world's largest cocaine producer, has evolved its drug policy significantly. Personal use of drugs has been decriminalized since the Constitutional Court's 1994 ruling (up to 20g marijuana, 1g cocaine). Colombia has shifted from aerial herbicide fumigation (glyphosate) toward voluntary crop substitution programs under the PDET plan for coca farmers. Under President Petro (2022+), Colombia has pursued 'total peace' negotiations with guerrilla and criminal groups including drug traffickers. Colombia's coca cultivation hit record levels despite decades of eradication efforts.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 10-30 years imprisonment; coca cultivation: eradication orders (not imprisonment for small farmers); personal use: decriminalized; drug lord asset forfeiture is a major enforcement tool
exceptions: Personal use decriminalized since 1994 Constitutional Court ruling
Small-scale coca farmers may join voluntary substitution programs with income support
Indigenous communities with traditional coca leaf use have protected rights
laws.sourceLabel: Colombia Constitutional Court Drug Ruling (1994) and PDET Program

quiz.q: Colombia's Constitutional Court decriminalized personal drug use in which year?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in 1994 that penalizing personal drug use violated individual rights to privacy and personal development, effectively decriminalizing possession of small amounts (up to 20g marijuana, 1g cocaine) — one of Latin America's earliest decriminalization decisions.

laws.title: Constitutional Court LGBTQ+ Rulings
laws.subtitle: Colombia's judicial path to LGBTQ+ equality
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitutional Court has been the primary engine of LGBTQ+ rights through a series of rulings. The Court recognized same-sex couples' benefits in 2007, granted adoption rights in 2015, and legalized same-sex marriage in 2016. Colombia also recognizes non-binary gender markers on ID documents. Constitutional Court ruling C-071/15 allowed single LGBTQ+ persons and same-sex couples to adopt. Colombia has a strong LGBTQ+ community in cities like Bogotá, Medellín, and Cali, though rural areas remain more conservative and violence against LGBTQ+ individuals is documented.
laws.penalty: LGBTQ+ discrimination in public services: civil and administrative action under anti-discrimination law; hate crimes against LGBTQ+: aggravated homicide/assault provisions; conversion therapy increasingly restricted
exceptions: Religious organizations retain some exemptions
Same-sex marriage not universally accessible in all regions due to bureaucratic resistance
Indigenous communities may have different frameworks under their special jurisdiction

quiz.q: Colombia's same-sex marriage was legalized in which year, through what mechanism?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in SU-214/16 (April 2016) that same-sex couples have the same right to marry as heterosexual couples, threatening that if Congress did not act by June 2016, notaries would begin issuing marriage certificates to same-sex couples — which they did.

laws.title: Press Freedom Challenges — Journalist Murders and Threats
laws.subtitle: Colombia has improved but journalists still face serious threats from armed groups
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's constitution protects freedom of the press (Article 20). Colombia has seen significant improvement in press freedom since the 1990s when journalists were routinely murdered by cartels and paramilitaries. However, journalists covering conflict zones, rural areas, and local corruption still face violence, particularly from FARC dissident groups, ELN guerrillas, and criminal organizations. The Foundation for Press Freedom (FLIP) documents ongoing threats. Digital surveillance of journalists is a concern. The peace process has improved conditions in some areas while creating new conflicts in others.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation law exists; journalist threats and murders remain a serious problem; formal censorship is prohibited
exceptions: Zones with armed conflict have severely restricted press freedom in practice

quiz.q: What organization in Colombia tracks and documents threats against journalists?
quiz.explanation: FLIP (Fundación para la Libertad de Prensa - Foundation for Press Freedom) is the leading Colombian organization documenting and responding to threats, attacks, and murders targeting journalists throughout the country.

laws.title: Habeas Data and Digital Privacy Protections
laws.subtitle: Colombia's constitutional right of habeas data governs personal data on digital platforms
laws.fullDescription: Colombia has a constitutional right of habeas data (Article 15), allowing citizens to access, update, and rectify their personal information. Law 1581 of 2012 regulates data protection for private entities including social media platforms. The Superintendence of Industry and Commerce (SIC) enforces data protection. Colombia has been active in the OAS and regional frameworks for digital governance. Social media platforms operate under habeas data requirements. Colombia's political polarization has made social media content moderation debates intense, particularly around elections and the peace process. Misinformation is a significant concern.
laws.penalty: Data protection violations: fines up to 2,000 minimum wages; SIC enforcement authority
exceptions: National security and journalism have some exemptions

quiz.q: What constitutional right does Colombia have regarding personal data that predates most countries' data protection laws?
options: A constitutional right to internet access
A constitutional right of habeas data (Article 15)
A constitutional ban on data mining
A constitutional right to anonymity online
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Article 15 of the constitution enshrines a right of habeas data — allowing citizens to access, update, and rectify their personal information held by any entity — a constitutional protection for data rights that predates GDPR and most modern data protection frameworks.

laws.title: Colombian Banking Regulation and Fintech Growth
laws.subtitle: Colombia has an active fintech sector and regulatory framework balancing innovation with stability
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's financial system is overseen by the Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia (SFC). Colombia has been expanding financial inclusion through digital banking — Nequi (Bancolombia's fintech) and Daviplata (Davivienda's) have millions of users. Colombia's Decree 1357 (2018) created a regulatory sandbox for fintech. The SFC has issued regulations on cryptocurrency for financial reporting. Colombia faces significant AML challenges from drug trafficking, with cartel proceeds infiltrating the financial system. Banco de la República is the central bank. Colombia's financial inclusion index has improved significantly through mobile banking.
laws.penalty: SFC regulatory enforcement; AML violations subject to criminal prosecution; sandbox participants have conditional exemptions
exceptions: State-owned financial entities have different regulatory treatment

quiz.q: What challenge does Colombia's financial system particularly face related to the drug trade?
options: Cartel proceeds infiltrating the banking system through money laundering
quiz.explanation: Colombia's financial system faces significant anti-money laundering challenges from drug trafficking — cartel proceeds from cocaine exports must be laundered, and Colombia's banking sector has historically been a target for infiltration, making AML compliance a critical regulatory priority.

laws.title: INVIMA Food Safety Regulation & Octagonal Warning Labels
laws.subtitle: Colombia's INVIMA regulates food safety for Latin America's third-largest food market
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's National Institute for Food and Drug Monitoring (INVIMA) regulates food safety, labeling, and market authorization for all processed foods. Colombia followed Mexico and Brazil in implementing octagonal front-of-package warning labels for foods exceeding nutritional thresholds, under Resolution 810 of 2021. INVIMA conducts food establishment inspections and oversees import/export of food products. The Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA) regulates agricultural inputs and exports. Colombia's food safety system must manage food security challenges in remote regions, where traditional food practices are common. Colombia has specific rules for its significant coffee export industry and for exotic Amazonian fruits increasingly sought by gourmet markets.
laws.penalty: INVIMA violations: fines from 1 to 10,000 monthly minimum wages; unauthorized food market entry: product confiscation and destruction; adulteration: criminal charges under Colombian Penal Code
exceptions: Traditional food products with geographic indications (café de Colombia, queso paipa) have modified production standards
Small artisanal producers below registration thresholds have simplified rules
Indigenous community food production for own consumption is exempt

quiz.q: What food product has Colombia obtained Protected Designation of Origin status for, protecting its premium market position?
quiz.explanation: 'Café de Colombia' has protected designation of origin status, and '100% Colombian Coffee' is one of the world's most recognized geographical indications. The Colombian Coffee Growers Federation has fought for and maintained this premium branding globally.

laws.title: Colombia Ley 1774 — Animals as Sentient Beings
laws.subtitle: Colombia constitutionally recognizes animal sentience
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Ley 1774 (2016) amended the Civil Code and Criminal Code to recognize animals as sentient beings — not mere property. The law creates criminal penalties for animal abuse for the first time and mandates progressive elimination of animal use in entertainment (bullfighting and cockfighting were grandfathered but are being phased out through local bans). Colombia's Constitutional Court has since ruled that animals have rights, and several court cases have explored habeas corpus for animals (including a famous case for a bear named Chucho). Local ordinances in Bogotá and Medellín add additional restrictions on horse-drawn vehicles, animal performances, and pet welfare.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties: 12–36 months imprisonment for abuse causing serious injury or death; up to 48 months for aggravated cruelty; fines of 5–60 minimum monthly wages
exceptions: Livestock production under ICA (national agricultural authority)
Scientific research with ethics committee approval
Approved sporting hunting
Bullfighting temporarily protected in traditional municipalities

quiz.q: What is significant about Colombia's Constitutional Court decisions regarding animals after Ley 1774?
options: Animals can vote in local elections
Courts have explored habeas corpus applications for individual animals
Animals are now represented in the Colombian Congress
quiz.explanation: After Ley 1774 recognized animal sentience, Colombia's Constitutional Court began examining habeas corpus applications for individual animals, including a case for a bear named Chucho — placing Colombia at the forefront of animal rights jurisprudence in Latin America.

laws.title: Colombia Family Law — Constitutional Court and Same-Sex Rights
laws.subtitle: Colombia's Constitutional Court progressively expanded LGBTQ+ family rights
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's family law is governed by the Civil Code and extensive Constitutional Court jurisprudence. Colombia's Constitutional Court has issued a series of landmark rulings expanding family rights for same-sex couples — equalizing inheritance rights (2007), pension rights (2008), adoption rights (2015), and ultimately ruling in 2016 that same-sex couples have the right to marry equally. The Civil Marriage Code requires civil ceremonies (religious marriages require additional civil registration). Colombia recognizes uniones maritales de hecho (unmarried unions) after 2 years of cohabitation, granting property rights. Child custody decisions are made by Family Defenders (Defensores de Familia) before going to court. Colombia's Family Code emphasizes children's rights extensively.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; alimentary obligations (support) can result in civil arrest for willful non-payment; contempt of court for violating protective orders
exceptions: Capitulaciones matrimoniales (prenuptial agreements)
Separate property regimes
Indigenous customary law recognized for indigenous communities
laws.sourceLabel: Código Civil Colombia — Derecho de Familia

quiz.q: How did Colombia achieve same-sex marriage — through legislature or courts?
options: Colombian Parliament voted for it in 2010
The President issued an executive decree
Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in 2016 that same-sex couples have the right to equal marriage
A national referendum approved it in 2015
quiz.explanation: Same-sex marriage in Colombia was achieved through Constitutional Court jurisprudence rather than legislation. After a series of rulings expanding same-sex couple rights, the Constitutional Court ruled in 2016 that denying equal marriage violated constitutional equality — making Colombia one of the first countries where courts rather than legislature drove marriage equality.

laws.title: Colombia Property Rights & Restitution Law
laws.subtitle: Land restitution for conflict-displaced victims
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Ley de Victimas y Restitucion de Tierras (Law 1448/2011) created a historic land restitution program for the approximately 7 million people displaced by the armed conflict, returning land seized by paramilitaries, guerrillas, and drug traffickers. The Unidad de Restitución de Tierras has processed hundreds of thousands of claims. The Civil Code also protects private property, while the 1991 Constitution's Article 58 affirms property rights balanced by the social function doctrine. Squatters can acquire property through acquisitive prescription after 10-20 years of peaceful, public possession.
laws.penalty: Land restitution: displaced persons receive title plus compensation; illegal dispossession is a criminal offense
exceptions: Restitution does not require proof of original title in conflict zones
Statute of limitations suspended during armed conflict
laws.source: Law 1448/2011; Constitucion Politica Art. 58; Codigo Civil

quiz.q: What was the primary purpose of Colombia's Law 1448 (2011)?
quiz.explanation: Law 1448 (Ley de Victimas) created Colombia's land restitution program specifically to return land seized from approximately 7 million people displaced by the internal armed conflict.

laws.title: Colombia Estatuto del Consumidor & SIC
laws.subtitle: Consumer rights statute and competition authority
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Estatuto del Consumidor (Law 1480/2011) comprehensively reformed consumer protection, providing rights to product safety, information, free choice, and effective complaint processes. The Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) serves as both consumer protection and competition authority. Consumers have a 5-day reversal right for distance purchases. The statute establishes strict product liability for manufacturers and distributors. Digital consumer rights are addressed through Resolution 20168-2016. Colombia's e-commerce sector has grown rapidly with Mercado Libre and Rappi, increasing the importance of online consumer protections.
laws.penalty: Product liability: solidarity between manufacturer and retailer; SIC fine up to 2,000 minimum wages; contract reversal for distance sales
exceptions: 5-day distance sale reversal right
SIC has both consumer protection and competition jurisdiction

quiz.q: What agency in Colombia enforces both consumer protection AND competition law?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) uniquely combines consumer protection enforcement with competition law authority — similar to the UK's CMA — giving it broad powers to address both individual consumer harms and market-level anticompetitive behavior.

laws.title: Proceso de Paz — FARC Peace Deal
laws.subtitle: 2016 Havana Peace Agreement — FARC demobilization
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2016 peace agreement with the FARC, signed in Havana after 4 years of negotiations under President Santos, ended 52 years of armed conflict. The deal included FARC disarmament, rural reform, drug substitution programs, transitional justice (Special Jurisdiction for Peace — JEP), political participation, and victim reparations. Over 13,000 FARC combatants demobilized. Santos won the Nobel Peace Prize. Implementation has been uneven — dissident FARC groups (FARC-EP) continue violence. A 2016 referendum initially rejected the deal (50.2%), which was then revised and ratified by Congress.
laws.penalty: FARC members who comply with JEP receive alternative sentences (no prison). Those who don't: regular criminal prosecution.
exceptions: JEP has jurisdiction until 2034 for transition period
Dissidents who rejected the agreement face regular justice
Former combatants receive economic reintegration support and security guarantees

quiz.q: What Nobel Prize did Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos receive for the FARC peace deal?
quiz.explanation: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos received the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize for his leadership in negotiating the Havana peace agreement with the FARC, ending 52 years of armed conflict. The committee noted that the agreement 'was the result of a long process that required courage, determination and leadership.'

laws.title: Federación Nacional de Cafeteros — Coffee Economy
laws.subtitle: FNC — Colombian coffee institution since 1927
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Federación Nacional de Cafeteros (FNC, 1927) is one of the world's largest rural NGOs, representing 540,000+ coffee-growing families. The FNC manages the Juan Valdez brand internationally, operates savings cooperatives, provides agronomic technical assistance, and maintains the Fondo Nacional del Café. Colombian coffee has Geographic Indication (GI) protection — Colombian Mild Arabicas are among the world's most valuable. Coffee represents about 7% of agricultural exports. The sector faces climate change challenges as optimal growing altitude bands shift upward.
laws.penalty: Misuse of GI 'Café de Colombia': civil and criminal penalties for fraud. Export certificate violations: fines and export suspension.
exceptions: Small producers (fewer than 5 hectares) have simplified market access programs
Organic certified coffee has premium price programs
Coffee grown outside designated regions cannot use GI designation

quiz.q: Approximately how many Colombian families does the Federación Nacional de Cafeteros represent?
quiz.explanation: The FNC represents over 540,000 Colombian coffee-growing families. As one of the world's largest rural NGOs, it provides technical assistance, manages the internationally recognized Juan Valdez brand, and operates the Fondo Nacional del Café, which stabilizes prices and invests in coffee communities.

laws.title: Ley 100 — Universal Health Insurance
laws.subtitle: Law 100/1993 — contributory and subsidized health regimes
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Law 100 (1993) created a universal health insurance system with two regimes: Contributivo (for formal workers, employer/employee funded) and Subsidiado (for informal/low-income, government funded). By 2015, coverage reached 97% — one of Latin America's highest. The Constitutional Court has been active in enforcing health rights through tutela (constitutional action). Colombia's health system is ranked relatively high among developing nations. The 2011 Ley Estatutaria de Salud declared health a fundamental right.
laws.penalty: Insurer denial of covered service: tutela action, daily fines. Employer non-contribution: back payments, penalties.
exceptions: Catastrophic illnesses covered by high-cost account (Cuenta de Alto Costo)
ARP (occupational risk) coverage separate from general health insurance
Military and police have separate health system (SANITAS/SISBEN)
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Salud — Sistema de Salud

quiz.q: What health coverage percentage did Colombia achieve by 2015 under its Law 100 system?
quiz.explanation: Colombia achieved approximately 97% health insurance coverage by 2015 — one of Latin America's highest rates — through the dual contributory/subsidized system created by Law 100 (1993). The Constitutional Court has been instrumental in enforcing health rights through tutela actions when insurers deny coverage.

laws.title: Tutela — Constitutional Protection Action
laws.subtitle: Article 86 Constitution — 10-day rights protection
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's tutela (Article 86, 1991 Constitution) is a fundamental rights protection mechanism. Any person can file a tutela when a fundamental constitutional right is violated or threatened, and the judge must respond within 10 days. No lawyer is required. Tutela is used over 600,000 times annually — mostly against healthcare insurers and public services. The Constitutional Court selects important tutelas for binding jurisprudence. Colombia's Constitutional Court is considered one of Latin America's most progressive, recognizing socioeconomic rights through tutela.
laws.penalty: Failure to comply with a tutela order: criminal contempt (contempt of court), disciplinary sanctions, and potential imprisonment of responsible official.
exceptions: Tutela cannot be used when other legal remedies haven't been tried (except when those remedies are inadequate)
Electoral actions excluded from tutela
Tutela cannot be filed against private parties unless they provide public services or are in dominant position

quiz.q: How quickly must a Colombian judge respond to a tutela (constitutional protection action)?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's tutela requires judges to respond within 10 calendar days — one of the fastest constitutional remedies in the world. The extreme speed and simplicity (no lawyer required) has made tutela Colombia's most-used legal mechanism, with over 600,000 filed annually.

laws.title: Amazon Deforestation — Páramo Protection
laws.subtitle: Constitutional rights of nature — rivers as legal persons
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled in 2018 that the Colombian Amazon has rights as a 'subject of rights' — a legal person deserving protection. This landmark ruling ordered the government to develop a 'Pacto Intergeneracional por la Vida del Amazonas Colombiano.' Colombia also protects páramos (high-altitude Andean wetland ecosystems) — mining and oil extraction are banned above 3,000-3,500m. Colombia is the world's second most biodiverse country. Deforestation in the Colombian Amazon doubled after the FARC demobilization as new actors colonized former conflict areas.
laws.penalty: Illegal deforestation: fines up to 15,000 SMLV (monthly wages), criminal prosecution 1-3 years. Páramo extraction: severe fines and criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Traditional indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities may continue subsistence activities
Pre-existing mining contracts in lower páramo areas have transition provisions
Scientific research with environmental authority permits allowed

quiz.q: What legal status did Colombia's Constitutional Court grant the Colombian Amazon in 2018?
quiz.explanation: In a landmark 2018 ruling, Colombia's Constitutional Court declared the Colombian Amazon a 'subject of rights' — a legal person with the right to protection, conservation, maintenance, and restoration. This is among the first rulings globally granting legal personhood to an ecosystem.

laws.title: Decreto 2535 — Civilian Arms Control
laws.subtitle: Decree 2535/1993 — military weapons ban for civilians
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Decree 2535 (1993) prohibited civilians from possessing weapons of war (military-grade firearms) and required permits for all civilian firearms from the Military Industry (INDUMIL). Colombia has extremely high armed conflict-related violence and civilian firearms contribute to an already severe homicide rate (~12,000 per year). The government periodically bans civilian carry in conflict-affected municipalities. Despite strict laws, illegal arms trafficking — often from FARC/ELN stocks — means illegal weapons are widely available.
laws.penalty: Illegal possession of war weapons: 9-12 years imprisonment. Carrying permitted firearm without authorization: 4-8 years.
exceptions: Security companies may possess regulated firearms for clients
Ranchers in rural conflict zones may request carry permits
Sport shooters and collectors may possess under permit with INDUMIL

quiz.q: What Colombian government entity issues civilian firearm permits?
quiz.explanation: In Colombia, civilian firearm permits are issued by INDUMIL (Industria Militar de Colombia) — the military industrial company. This centralized military control of civilian firearms reflects the security concerns of a country with a long armed conflict history.

laws.title: Hacienda Pública — Tax Reform 2022
laws.subtitle: 2022 tax reform — progressive income and wealth taxes
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2022 tax reform under President Petro increased taxes on high incomes, expanded the dividend tax, introduced a new wealth tax (over 3 billion pesos in assets), and added export taxes on oil and coal. The reform also eliminated some corporate tax exemptions. The oil export tax was controversial — oil represents 30% of Colombia's exports. The reform aimed to raise 20 trillion pesos annually to fund social programs. Critics argued it would reduce investment; supporters argued Colombia's tax burden (19% of GDP) was among Latin America's lowest.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: criminal prosecution, fines, interest. Corporate tax fraud: company dissolution.
exceptions: Small businesses (microempresas) have simplified tax regimes
Agricultural cooperatives have modified tax treatment
Free trade zones have special tax regimes
laws.sourceLabel: DIAN — Dirección de Impuestos y Aduanas Nacionales

quiz.q: What was the 2022 Colombian tax reform's new wealth tax threshold (asset value)?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's 2022 tax reform under President Petro introduced a wealth tax on individuals and companies with assets exceeding 3 billion Colombian pesos (approximately $750,000 USD). The reform also increased dividend taxes and added export taxes on oil and coal.

laws.title: Consulta Previa — Indigenous Prior Consultation
laws.subtitle: ILO 169 — mandatory consultation for indigenous communities
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitution (Article 330) and ILO Convention 169 (ratified 1991) require free, prior, and informed consultation with indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities before any project affecting their territories. The Constitutional Court has ruled that consultation must be in good faith and may result in veto power for some decisions. Over 85 ethnic groups and 700+ indigenous reserves exist in Colombia. Afro-Colombian communities (comunidades negras) have collective land rights under Law 70/1993. Mining and infrastructure projects routinely require extensive consultation processes.
laws.penalty: Projects proceeding without required consultation: suspension orders, project nullification. Companies face civil liability for harm to communities.
exceptions: Emergency situations may have expedited procedures
Projects exclusively on non-indigenous/non-collective territory don't require consultation
Consultation requirements vary based on impact significance

quiz.q: What international convention ratified by Colombia requires prior consultation with indigenous communities?
quiz.explanation: ILO Convention 169, ratified by Colombia in 1991, is the primary international framework for indigenous prior consultation rights. Combined with Colombia's 1991 Constitution Article 330, it requires free, prior, and informed consultation with indigenous communities before projects affecting their territories.

laws.title: Marco Jurídico para la Paz — Transitional Justice
laws.subtitle: Constitutional framework for transitional justice
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's 2012 Marco Jurídico para la Paz constitutional amendment created the framework for transitional justice in the peace process. It enabled the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), which operates as a temporary special court for conflict-related crimes. The JEP can impose non-prison sentences (restricted liberty, community service, land restoration) for those who confess fully. It also created the Truth Commission (Comisión de la Verdad) and the Unit for the Search of Missing Persons (UBPD). The JEP has jurisdiction over military members, FARC, and third parties (civilians and companies).
laws.penalty: JEP participants who lie or fail to comply: reclassified to regular criminal justice. Military members: regular military justice for non-compliant.
exceptions: Crimes against humanity and war crimes that are not confessed receive up to 20 years
laws.sourceLabel: Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz — JEP

quiz.q: What is the maximum prison sentence under JEP for fully confessed conflict crimes?
quiz.explanation: Under the JEP (Special Jurisdiction for Peace), those who fully confess their conflict-related crimes receive alternative non-prison sentences — restricted liberty, community service, or land restoration work. Prison sentences (up to 20 years) apply only to those who don't confess or who lie to the tribunal.

laws.title: Pico y Placa — Bogotá Vehicle Circulation Restriction
laws.subtitle: License plate-based traffic rationing in Bogotá
laws.fullDescription: Bogotá's Pico y Placa (Peak and Plate) program restricts vehicle circulation based on the last digit of the license plate, varying by day of week, during morning and afternoon peak hours. The system aims to reduce traffic congestion in one of the world's most congested cities. High-occupancy vehicles (3+ passengers), electric vehicles, and public transit are exempt. Multiple exemptions apply. Other Colombian cities (Medellín, Cali) have similar systems. Pico y Placa has been periodically expanded and modified since its 1998 introduction.
laws.penalty: Circulating during restricted hours: traffic fine (comparendo), typically $600,000-800,000 COP.
exceptions: Electric and hybrid vehicles generally exempt
High-occupancy vehicles (3+ passengers) exempt
Emergency vehicles, diplomatic vehicles, motorcycles have specific exemptions

quiz.q: Bogotá's Pico y Placa system restricts vehicle circulation based on what?
options: Last digit of license plate number
quiz.explanation: Bogotá's Pico y Placa restricts vehicles based on the last digit of the license plate number. Different digits are restricted on different days of the week during peak hours. The system has been in operation since 1998 and has been widely replicated in other Colombian cities and Latin American capitals.

laws.title: Zonas Francas — Free Trade Zones
laws.subtitle: Law 1004/2005 — special economic zones
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's free trade zones (Zonas Francas) operate under Law 1004/2005, offering companies a flat 20% corporate income tax rate (vs. 35% general), exemption from import duties on goods brought into the zone, and simplified customs procedures. Colombia has 105+ free trade zones — permanent (large industrial), special (single project), and coastal. Key sectors: textiles, pharma, technology. PROCOLOMBIA promotes foreign investment. Companies in zonas francas must export at least 60% of output (industrial) or provide national interest services.
laws.penalty: Violating zona franca regime (selling domestically above threshold): back duties and taxes, regime suspension.
exceptions: Service free trade zones have no minimum export requirement
Health tourism zones have distinct regulations
Some zonas francas have additional incentives for specific sectors

quiz.q: What corporate income tax rate applies to companies operating in Colombian free trade zones?
quiz.explanation: Companies operating in Colombia's zonas francas (free trade zones) pay a flat corporate income tax rate of 20%, compared to the general 35% rate. They also enjoy exemption from import duties on goods brought into the zone, making them attractive for export-oriented manufacturing and services.

laws.title: RAMV — Venezuelan Migrant Registry
laws.subtitle: Venezuela migration — Colombia hosts 2+ million
laws.fullDescription: Colombia hosts approximately 2.8 million Venezuelan migrants — the largest Venezuelan diaspora worldwide. In response, Colombia created the Temporary Protection Status (ETPV — Estatuto Temporal de Protección) in 2021, offering a 10-year renewable residency permit to Venezuelans. This allowed Venezuelans to work legally, access healthcare, and enroll children in schools. The RAMV (Registry of Venezuelan Migrants) preceded the ETPV. Colombia has been praised internationally for this open-door approach while simultaneously experiencing internal pressure as the large influx strains services.
laws.penalty: Irregular status: deportation risk. ETPV violations: status revocation.
exceptions: Venezuelans with regular migration status (visas) can pursue permanent residency through normal channels
Children born in Colombia to Venezuelan parents have Colombian citizenship rights
UNHCR recognized refugees have separate status

quiz.q: Approximately how many Venezuelan migrants does Colombia host?
quiz.explanation: Colombia hosts approximately 2.8 million Venezuelan migrants — the largest Venezuelan diaspora in the world. In 2021, Colombia created the Temporary Protection Status (ETPV) offering 10-year renewable residency permits to Venezuelans, allowing them to work legally and access public services.

laws.title: Colombia Cultural Policy — Law of Culture
laws.subtitle: Law 397/1997 — cultural rights and heritage protection
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Ley General de Cultura (Law 397/1997) establishes culture as a fundamental constitutional right and the basis of Colombian nationality. It created the Ministry of Culture, the National Cultural Heritage Council, and cultural regional funds. Colombia's UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Old City of Cartagena, Los Katíos National Park, and the Coffee Cultural Landscape. The National Plan for Culture guides state cultural investment. Colombia is also internationally recognized for its literary and artistic heritage (Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize, Botero).
laws.penalty: Destruction of cultural heritage: criminal prosecution (3-8 years) and civil damages. Unauthorized export of cultural property: confiscation.
exceptions: Archaeological heritage (subsoil) belongs to the state regardless of land ownership
Indigenous cultural heritage has community governance
Colonial religious art may have church-state agreements

quiz.q: Which Colombian author's Nobel Prize for Literature is part of Colombia's internationally recognized cultural heritage?
quiz.explanation: Gabriel García Márquez received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982 for his magical realism works, most famously 'One Hundred Years of Solitude.' He is Colombia's most internationally recognized cultural figure. Note: Borges was Argentine, Neruda was Chilean, and Vargas Llosa was Peruvian.

laws.title: Biodiversidad — Biopiracy Protections
laws.subtitle: Decision 391 — genetic resources sovereignty
laws.fullDescription: Colombia is the world's second most biodiverse country per unit area. Andean Community Decision 391 (1996) establishes national sovereignty over genetic resources and requires prior informed consent and benefit sharing for access. Bioprospecting without authorization is prohibited. Colombia has ratified the Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing. IAVH (Alexander von Humboldt Biological Resources Research Institute) manages biodiversity inventories. Traditional knowledge of indigenous communities is protected from biopiracy.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized bioprospecting: fines, research suspension, criminal prosecution. Biopiracy: civil liability for benefits derived.
exceptions: Academic research with benefit-sharing agreements
Traditional communities retain rights to commercialize their own knowledge
Seed exchange between farmers exempt from some regulations

quiz.q: By what international ranking is Colombia considered the world's second most biodiverse country?
quiz.explanation: Colombia is ranked the world's second most biodiverse country when measured by biodiversity per unit area. Despite being only 0.77% of Earth's landmass, Colombia contains approximately 10% of all species on Earth, including more bird species than any other country.

laws.title: Ley de Inteligencia — Intelligence Oversight
laws.subtitle: Law 1621/2013 — intelligence framework and oversight
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Law 1621/2013 established the legal framework for intelligence and counterintelligence activities. The DAS (Directorate of Administrative Security), which had conducted illegal surveillance on journalists, judges, and opposition figures, was dissolved in 2011. Intelligence functions were redistributed to the CNI (National Intelligence Directorate). The law prohibits intelligence activities based on political beliefs, ethnicity, religion, or union membership. A 2016 scandal revealed the military 'ANDROMEDA' project had conducted mass phone surveillance.
laws.penalty: Illegal intelligence operations: criminal prosecution of officers, civil liability. Unauthorized sharing of intelligence: 4-8 years.
exceptions: Judicial authorization required for communication interception
Emergency threat situations may allow temporary surveillance without prior authorization
Anti-terrorism operations have broader intelligence powers

quiz.q: Which Colombian intelligence agency was dissolved in 2011 after conducting illegal surveillance?
quiz.explanation: The DAS (Departamento Administrativo de Seguridad) was dissolved in 2011 after revelations that it had conducted illegal surveillance on journalists, judges, human rights defenders, and opposition politicians. Its legitimate intelligence functions were redistributed to new agencies, including the CNI.

laws.title: Restitución de Tierras — Land Restitution
laws.subtitle: Law 1448/2010 — Victims and Land Restitution Law
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Law 1448 (Victims and Land Restitution Law, 2010) created a process to restore land to those displaced by armed conflict. An estimated 7 million Colombians were displaced from 7+ million hectares of land. The Unit for Land Restitution processes claims and specialized courts adjudicate them. By 2023, approximately 300,000 hectares had been formally restored to victims — a fraction of total claims. Claimants face security threats from armed groups controlling formerly dispossessed land.
laws.penalty: Obstructing land restitution: criminal prosecution. Violence against claimants or restitution judges: aggravated penalties.
exceptions: Third parties who legally acquired land in good faith have some protections
Collective restitution for indigenous/Afro communities follows separate procedures
Strategic projects (infrastructure, mining) on claimed land may have priority reviews

quiz.q: Approximately how many Colombians were displaced by armed conflict and are eligible for land restitution?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 7 million Colombians were forcibly displaced by armed conflict — primarily by paramilitary groups (AUC) and guerrillas (FARC, ELN). Law 1448 created the land restitution process, but only a fraction of displaced land has been formally restored due to security threats, institutional capacity limits, and opposing interests.

laws.title: ETCR — Former Combatant Reintegration
laws.subtitle: Territories for Training and Reincorporation
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's ETCR (Espacios Territoriales de Capacitación y Reincorporación) are rural communities where former FARC combatants reintegrate into civilian life. Created as part of the 2016 peace deal, ETCRs provide housing, vocational training, and economic projects for former combatants and their families. The National Reintegration Council (CNR) oversees the process. Security in and around ETCRs has been precarious — former combatants face threats from FARC dissidents, ELN, and criminal organizations. Over 13,000 former FARC members entered the reintegration process.
laws.penalty: Former combatants who abandon the reintegration process and rejoin armed groups: prosecution under regular criminal law.
exceptions: Former combatants receive economic support for 24 months
Children associated with FARC have special protection protocols
Combatants with pending international arrest warrants have protected status during transition

quiz.q: How many former FARC members entered Colombia's reintegration process after the 2016 peace deal?
quiz.explanation: Over 13,000 former FARC combatants entered Colombia's reintegration process after the 2016 Havana peace agreement. They were concentrated in Espacios Territoriales de Capacitación y Reincorporación (ETCRs), receiving economic support, vocational training, and legal protection through the JEP transitional justice system.

laws.title: Minería — Mining Law and Royalties
laws.subtitle: Law 685/2001 Mining Code — royalty reform
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Mining Code (Law 685/2001) established the regulatory framework for mining. The 2011 royalty reform (Legislative Act 05) redistributed royalties from producing regions to a national fund serving all departments — a major political controversy. Colombia has significant gold, coal, nickel, and emerald reserves. Emeralds from Muzo and Coscuez supply 55% of the world's emeralds. Illegal artisanal mining (barequeo) is regulated differently. Mining in environmental protection areas, páramos, and indigenous territories is prohibited.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining: 2-8 years imprisonment, equipment confiscation. Environmental damage from mining: additional criminal charges.
exceptions: Artisanal subsistence mining (barequeo) has simplified registration
Small-scale mining has transitional legalization programs
Foreign mining companies with pre-existing contracts grandfather some rights

quiz.q: What percentage of the world's emeralds come from Colombia's mines?
quiz.explanation: Colombia produces approximately 55% of the world's emeralds, primarily from the mines of Muzo, Coscuez, and Chivor in the Boyacá department. Colombian emeralds are world-renowned for their quality and intense green color.

laws.title: Rights of LGBT Persons — Constitutional Court Jurisprudence
laws.subtitle: Colombia's progressive court-led LGBT equality
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitutional Court has been a global pioneer in LGBT rights through progressive rulings: same-sex couples recognized with marriage rights (2016), adoption by same-sex couples permitted (2015), gender marker change without surgery (2015), pension rights for same-sex partners (2007). Colombia does not have comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation but constitutional protection applies. Trans women face disproportionate violence — Colombia has one of the highest rates of trans homicide in Latin America. LGBTI homicides increased during 2022-2023.
laws.penalty: Discrimination based on sexual orientation by public entities: constitutional action (tutela). Violence: criminal law penalties with possible hate crime aggravation.
exceptions: Religious institutions may maintain traditional positions in internal matters
Private clubs have some freedom of association
Conscientious objection for individual officials remains contested

quiz.q: In what year did Colombia's Constitutional Court recognize same-sex marriage rights?
quiz.explanation: Colombia's Constitutional Court recognized same-sex marriage rights in 2016, following a series of progressive rulings on LGBT rights. The Court found that barring same-sex couples from marriage violated constitutional equality principles. Colombia legalized same-sex marriage through court decision rather than legislative action.

laws.title: Paro Nacional — Right to Strike and Protest
laws.subtitle: Constitutional right to strike; labor disputes and 2021 protests
laws.fullDescription: Colombia's Constitution guarantees the right to strike, with exceptions for essential services. The 2021 Paro Nacional (national strike) began May 1 against a proposed tax reform and escalated into weeks of protests over inequality, police violence, and social spending cuts. The Human Rights Unit documented at least 44 deaths during the protests, with ESMAD (riot police) facing serious accusations. The Petro government (2022) has sought to restrict ESMAD's use of certain weapons. Colombia has a long history of labor strikes affecting the oil sector, transportation, and agriculture.
laws.penalty: Illegal strike in essential services: civil liability for damages. Blocking roads during strikes: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Essential services (health, water, electricity) have regulated strike procedures
Strikes may be declared illegal by Ministry of Labor
Solidarity strikes are restricted

quiz.q: What triggered Colombia's 2021 Paro Nacional (national strike)?
options: A proposed tax reform under President Duque
The murder of a prominent politician
A constitutional amendment on presidential reelection
quiz.explanation: The 2021 Paro Nacional began on May 1 (Labor Day) triggered by President Duque's proposed tax reform, which would have expanded the tax base to middle-class Colombians. It escalated into weeks of protests over deeper issues including inequality, lack of opportunities, police violence, and the slow implementation of the 2016 peace agreement.
